modules.title: Formative assessment as the engine of the classroom
modules.hook: Ruth Butler handed back students' work in three ways: comments only, grades only, or grades plus comments. Only one group improved on the next task. Which one, and what does that do to the gradebook you were planning to build?

attempt.prompt: Write a single multiple-choice question (four options) for the end of a Year 8 lesson on photosynthesis. Its job: tell the teacher, in under a minute, whether to move on tomorrow or reteach. Then, for each wrong option, write one sentence on what a student who picks it must be thinking and what the teacher should do about it. Finally, write one sentence on how the school would make sure every teacher actually uses questions like this, not just on the day of the training. Do it cold; you will compare it to the design rules below.

objectives: Explain what makes an assessment formative (the decision it changes, not the instrument), and why the short cycle carries most of the value.
Write a hinge question whose every distractor diagnoses a named misconception, with a pre-set decision threshold.
Design a grading and feedback policy grounded in Kluger & DeNisi and Butler, and say which parts are evidence and which are cadence guesses.
Design a teacher learning community (TLC) that changes habits rather than shares ideas, using choice, flexibility, small steps, accountability and support.
State a realistic whole-school effect size for formative assessment (about 0.1 SD at scale) and explain why the famous 1998 numbers were larger.

ideas.title: Formative is a use of evidence, not a kind of test
ideas.body:
Most people hear *assessment* and think *test*. Wiliam and Leahy move the word from the instrument to the decision: an assessment is formative **to the extent that** evidence of learning is elicited, interpreted and used, by the teacher, the student or a peer, to make a better next step than would have been made without it. The same ten-question quiz is formative on Monday if the teacher regroups students on Tuesday because of it, and merely summative if the scores go into a tracker nobody opens until report cards.

**Three cycle lengths.** Long cycle (terms, across units); medium cycle (within and between units, days to weeks); short cycle (minute by minute, day by day). Most school data systems, such as benchmark tests and termly dashboards, run on the long cycle and rarely change Thursday's lesson. The payoff concentrates in the short cycle, because that is where decisions about the students in front of you actually change. Product analogy: the quarterly revenue report versus an alert that fires while the incident is still live. Both are data; only one changes what you do in time.

**Decision-driven data collection.** Reverse the usual order. Do not collect data and then ask what it means. Name the decision first (move on or reteach? which four students need me at the back table?) and design the smallest piece of evidence that informs it. This one habit prevents most dashboards nobody acts on.

**Where the idea came from, and how big the effect really is.** Scriven (1967) distinguished formative from summative evaluation of curricula; Bloom carried the word into mastery learning. Black & Wiliam's 1998 review of roughly 250 studies (popularized as *Inside the Black Box*) reported gains typically around 0.4 to 0.7 SD, largest for lower achievers. That number built a movement, and it is too high to plan with. It came from a narrative synthesis, not a formal meta-analysis. Bennett (2011) called the concept ill-defined; Kingston & Nash (2011) found a weighted mean nearer 0.2 and few high-quality studies. Wiliam has conceded the 1998 figures were not precise estimates. The KMOFAP project (1999-2001, about 24 maths and science teachers) found roughly 0.3 SD on external measures, and its main lesson was that teachers could not simply be told the research; they had to rebuild practice in their own rooms over time.

The strongest test is the **EEF randomized trial of the Embedding Formative Assessment programme**: 140 English secondary schools, about 25,000 pupils, monthly TLC workshops run from resource packs, plus peer observation. Result: about **two months' additional progress** on GCSE Attainment 8 (effect about 0.09; 0.11 excluding schools already running something similar), with a very high security rating.

**How to hold this.** Plan for roughly 0.1 SD across a whole school over two years from a cheap, scalable programme. That is not magic, but at its cost it is among the best bets available (Module 8 does the comparison). Treat anyone promising 0.5 at scale as a vendor, not a researcher; the fall from 0.4-0.7 in small studies to about 0.1 at scale is ordinary scale-up decay, not failure.

**Folk theory to retire:** formative means low-stakes quizzes plus a data platform. Stakes and frequency do not define it; use does. Frequent *grading* can even do harm (see the feedback idea below).

ideas.title: Make every student's thinking visible: hinge questions and the elicitation toolkit
ideas.body:
Teaching is contingent: you cannot choose the next move without knowing what students currently think. The default classroom gets that evidence from raised hands, meaning the three confident volunteers. That is a biased sample, like a satisfaction survey only happy customers answer. A teacher who hears three right answers and moves on has learned almost nothing about the other 27.

**The core techniques**
- **No hands up.** Hands are for asking, not answering. The teacher chooses, often at random (named sticks, a randomizer). Everyone has to think because anyone may be called, and the teacher gets a representative sample. Pair it with norms like *I don't know yet, come back to me* or it becomes a status threat, which Yeager (Module 3) predicts adolescents will resist.
- **Wait time.** Mary Budd Rowe found teachers typically wait about one second after asking; three seconds or more produces longer, better answers and wider participation. Probably the cheapest intervention in this course.
- **All-student response.** Mini-whiteboards, ABCD cards, finger votes, polls. Everyone answers at once, so you see a distribution, not an anecdote.
- **Exit tickets.** One question at the door; sort answers into piles; tomorrow's opening changes. If tomorrow does not change, it was a ritual.
- **Interpretive listening** (Brent Davis): listen to understand what the student is thinking, not only to check whether they said the answer you were waiting for.

**The hinge question: the smallest complete unit of formative assessment.** It sits at the point where the lesson forks. Design rules: every student answers; students need about a minute; you can read the room in about 30 seconds; it is hard to get right for the wrong reason; and, the rule most people miss, **every wrong option maps to a specific, known misconception**, so a wrong answer tells you *what* to fix, not only *that* something is wrong. Set the threshold before you ask (for example: if nearly all are right, move on and pull the few aside; otherwise reteach a different way).

This is where Module 2 pays off. Shtulman, Vosniadou and Posner showed that wrong answers are systematic; they come from coherent intuitive theories. **A good distractor is a named intuitive theory.** For photosynthesis, the option *most of a tree's mass comes from the soil* is the soil-as-food theory that van Helmont's willow experiment overturned. A recall question (*which gas do plants take in?*) cannot catch it: a student can recite *carbon dioxide* and still believe the mass comes from the ground, which is Vosniadou's synthetic model in action.

**Institutional move.** Diagnostic questions are hard to invent live, so treat them as **curriculum assets**: a school-owned bank of hinge questions per unit, each with its distractor rationales, maintained like a shared test suite and improved when data shows a distractor nobody picks. Put whiteboards in every room. Make no-hands-up and all-student response school-wide defaults so students meet the same routine in every class.

**Evidence honesty.** Wait time and the general value of eliciting and using evidence have research behind them. Most named techniques (hinge questions, exit tickets, lolly sticks) are practitioner-derived and have not been isolated in randomized trials. They are bets grounded in mechanism and in the tested package, not individually proven components. Tag the bank [H], the principle [E].

ideas.title: Feedback can hurt: grades, comments, and what the student does next
ideas.body:
Feedback feels obviously good. The evidence says it is a powerful drug with a real rate of harmful side effects.

**Kluger & DeNisi (1996).** A meta-analysis of about 600 effect sizes. Feedback improved performance on average, but in roughly **38% of cases it made performance worse**. The pattern: feedback that directs attention to the self (praise, ranking, ego, *you're so clever*) tends to hurt; feedback directed at the task and how to improve it tends to help. Hattie & Timperley (2007) give the complementary levels: task, process, self-regulation, self. The self level is the weakest.

**Butler (1987/1988).** Students got comments only, grades only, or grades plus comments. Only the comments-only group improved. Adding a grade wiped out the comment: students look at the number, compare it with a neighbor's, and stop reading. Hence **comment-only marking** on formative work, or grades delayed until the student has acted on the comments. Caveat: Butler's samples were small and specific; the pattern has been conceptually replicated rather than tested at scale.

**Feedback is defined by use.** Ramaprasad (1983): feedback is information about the gap between where the learner is and where they need to be, *used to close that gap*. Information nobody uses is not feedback; it is data. Two practical rules follow. Feedback should be **more work for the recipient than the donor**, and it should look forward (what to do next) rather than narrate what went wrong. Think of a coach's correction, not a verdict.

**Techniques that make students do the work**
- **Find it and fix it**: tell the student there are five errors in this section, not where they are.
- **Focused marking**: comment on one or two criteria, not everything.
- **Whole-class feedback**: read the whole set, write the four or five most common issues on the board, each student decides which apply and redrafts.
- **Protected redraft time** in lessons, so acting on feedback is part of the timetable, not homework that never happens.

**Relationship is part of the mechanism.** The same comment can motivate or deflate depending on whether the student believes the teacher thinks they can improve. Yeager's wise-feedback study (Module 3) is the sharpest demonstration: a short note stating high standards and belief in the student raised essay revision among Black seventh graders from about 17% to about 71%. Boekaerts' model explains why: at every moment a student is choosing between a growth pathway (engage with the task) and a well-being pathway (protect myself). Rankings, public leaderboards and frequent grades push students toward self-protection, which looks like laziness from the front of the room.

**Policy consequences for your school.** Judge marking by what students do with it, not by how much red ink teachers produce. Ban or delay grades on formative work; require a student response to feedback; build redraft time into lessons. A bonus a product person will appreciate: this *reduces* teacher workload, because detailed written marking that nobody acts on is the most expensive low-value activity in most schools.

**Folk theory to retire:** more feedback, and more detailed feedback, is always better. Volume is not the variable. Focus, task orientation, trust, and a required student action are.

ideas.title: Clear targets, and students as resources for each other and owners of their learning
ideas.body:
The five strategies come from a simple grid (Leahy, Lyon, Thompson & Wiliam 2005; Thompson & Wiliam 2008): three processes (where the learner is going, where the learner is now, how to get there) crossed with three agents (teacher, peer, learner). The teacher-side strategies are **clarify intentions and success criteria**, **elicit evidence**, and **give feedback that moves learning forward**. The other two put students to work: **peers as learning resources** and **learners as owners of their learning**. One big idea sits over all five: use evidence of learning to adapt teaching to meet learning needs. The grid is useful as a shared observation and planning language across every subject.

**Strategy 1: students cannot hit a target they cannot see.** Many students, disproportionately disadvantaged ones, fail not from lack of ability but from not knowing what quality looks like in a domain. But copying an objective off the board is an empty ritual; the aim is understanding, not announcement. Four distinctions do the work:
- **Learning intention vs. task.** *Make a poster about volcanoes* is an activity. What is to be learned?
- **Context-specific vs. context-free.** *Write to the council about the skate park* vs. *use evidence to support a claim*. Make the transferable intention visible so learning generalizes.
- **Product vs. process criteria**: what finished work looks like vs. what you do to get there. Rubrics that say *some detail* vs. *a lot of detail* are close to useless.
- **Exemplars beat descriptors.** Quality in complex work is often tacit (Sadler's guild knowledge). Students learn it by comparing and ranking real samples of work.
You may delay announcing the intention when announcing it would spoil an inquiry (this is where Kapur's generate-first lessons fit); the requirement is that by the end students know what they learned.

**Strategy 4: peers as resources.** One teacher cannot give 28 students enough feedback. Slavin's synthesis sets the conditions for group work to beat individual work: **group goals** (the group succeeds together) *and* **individual accountability** (each member's learning counts, so nobody free-rides). Without both, group work is often worse than working alone. Peer assessment helps the *assessor* at least as much as the assessed, because judging work against criteria builds the sense of quality that self-assessment needs. Tools: two stars and a wish, pre-flight checklists before submission, reporter chosen at random from the group.

**Strategy 5: learners as owners.** The long-run target is self-regulated learners who monitor their own understanding and pick strategies. Self-assessment is a skill that must be taught with criteria and exemplars; until then students' self-reports are poorly calibrated. Motivation is as much an outcome of successful learning as a cause of it (this echoes Module 3). Watch **traffic lights**, the classic lethal mutation: students show red, amber or green cards, the teacher never acts on the signal, and students learn to show green to avoid attention.

**Design implications.** Curriculum documents should separate intentions from tasks and ship annotated exemplars at several quality levels [H]. All group work is designed with group goals plus individual accountability [E, Slavin]. Peer and self assessment are taught as explicit skills with common school-wide protocols from the early grades [H]. Minimize ego-involving displays such as public rankings and ability-labelled tables [E for the mechanism, V for the choice].

ideas.title: Teachers change habits, not knowledge: the teacher learning community
ideas.body:
This is the institutional half of the argument, and the reason Module 6 bridges into Institutions. The claim: teachers do not lack knowledge; they lack a way to change **habits**. Teaching is a real-time performance with hundreds of decisions an hour, most of them automatic. Knowing about hinge questions does not make you use one at minute 23 of a messy lesson, any more than reading about a golf swing changes yours. One-off workshops, conferences and inspirational speakers transmit knowledge and change little. Habit change needs practice in your own classroom, repeated over months, with follow-up, for about two years.

**Five design principles for teacher change**: **choice** (teachers pick the techniques that fit their room), **flexibility** (adapt within limits), **small steps** (one or two changes at a time), **accountability** (commit to colleagues and report back; accountability for trying and reflecting, not for outcomes), and **support** (time, peers, materials, leadership backing).

**The standard TLC spec**
- **Size**: about 8-12 teachers. Smaller gets fragile when people are absent; larger leaves no time for everyone to report. Mixed subjects are fine, because the shared content is pedagogy. Led by a trained teacher leader who facilitates rather than lectures.
- **Cadence**: monthly, roughly 75-120 minutes, for about two years. Monthly because teachers need three or four weeks to try a technique repeatedly; more often means nothing to report, less often means momentum dies.
- **Agenda**: introduction; a short starter; **How's it going?** (the heart, often half the meeting: each teacher reports what they committed to try, what happened, what they would change); new learning; **personal action planning** (write down the technique for next month, and sometimes what you will stop doing to make room); review.
- **Between meetings**: peer observation focused on what the *observed* teacher asked to be watched for. Developmental, never evaluative.

**Tight but loose** (Thompson & Wiliam 2008). Be tight on the core theory (the big idea and five strategies) and on process (meetings, plans, observation). Be loose on which techniques each teacher adopts. Too tight kills ownership; too loose breeds **lethal mutations**, where a technique keeps its name and loses its active ingredient: no hands up where the same three students are always picked; traffic lights nobody acts on. Product analogy: tight on the API contract, loose on the implementation, with tests that check the contract.

**Why it works (the causal story).** Repeated trial in real classrooms at spaced intervals targets habit directly; saying in front of colleagues that you will try something creates supportive accountability; improvement becomes normal rather than remedial; and packaged materials make it cheap to run without scarce experts. Evidence: the TLC model came out of ETS's Keeping Learning on Track work and was tested in the EEF trial described above (140 schools, about two months' extra progress). Which ingredients are necessary has not been isolated, so the parameters (size, cadence) are sensible defaults to tune [H], not optimized constants.

**Leadership requirements.** Protect the time, usually by stopping lower-value things such as routine meetings or volume marking. Never use TLC content in performance evaluation [H: psychological-safety reasoning, not directly tested]. Keep the agenda on formative practice and do not let it drift into logistics. Wiliam's refrain: every teacher needs to improve, not because they are not good enough, but because they can always be better.

worked_example.title: Decision: the school's assessment, feedback and teacher-learning policy
steps: Start from the mechanism, not the tool. Kluger & DeNisi show feedback can lower performance when it points at the self; Butler shows grades cancel comments. So the policy question is not how much feedback but what kind, and what the student must do with it. [E]

Formative work gets comments only; grades appear at a small number of summative points per term, and only after students have acted on the comments for that unit. [E for the mechanism; H for how many summative points, which you will tune]

Every comment requires a student action in lesson time: redraft, find-and-fix, or answer three targeted questions. Marking is judged by the student response it produces, not by volume. Written marking load drops, which is itself a reason teachers will accept the policy. [E for task-focused feedback; H for the specific routines]

Every lesson contains at least one planned, all-student evidence point, a hinge question or whiteboard check, with a threshold set before it is asked; exit tickets are sorted and change the next lesson's opening. [E for eliciting and using evidence; H for this cadence]
The school owns a hinge-question bank per unit with distractor rationales keyed to named misconceptions from the conceptual-change literature, reviewed each term using response data. [H]

Success criteria are shared through annotated exemplars at several quality levels, co-constructed with students where possible; planning templates separate the learning intention from the task. [E for exemplars and criteria clarity; H for the template]

Every teacher joins a TLC: 8-12 people, monthly, 90 minutes, a two-year arc, the standard agenda, a personal action plan, and one peer observation per month on the observed teacher's chosen focus. Time comes from cancelling one routine meeting a month. TLC content never enters appraisal. [E for the package (EEF trial); H for the parameters; V for keeping it separate from evaluation]

Set expectations in writing: the target is about 0.1 SD of whole-school gain over two years, measured on the external measure, with hinge-question distractor rates and redraft rates as leading indicators. [E for the realistic effect size; H for the leading indicators]
Policy line for the brief: Formative work is for learning, so it gets comments that students must act on; teachers get better together, monthly, for years.

hinge.q: Which of these is a formative use of a test?
options: A quiz whose results the teacher uses to regroup students for the next two lessons, because the evidence changed what happens next
Any quiz that is low-stakes and not recorded, because removing the grade is what turns a measurement into a learning event
A quiz the teacher wrote herself rather than one from an external body, because only the author knows what the items are probing
A quiz returned with scores so students know where they stand, because feedback on standing is what lets students adjust their effort
diagnoses: Correct. Formative is defined by use: evidence was elicited, interpreted, and it changed what happens next for specific students.
Stakes define formativeness. Low stakes help, but a low-stakes quiz whose results change nothing is not formative, and a high-stakes test can be used formatively.
Authorship defines formativeness. Who wrote the instrument is irrelevant; what matters is whether the evidence changes the next decision.
Information-to-student equals formative. Knowing where you stand changes nothing unless someone makes a different next-step decision; a bare score can even push students into ego-involvement.

hinge.q: A hinge question is well designed if:
options: About half the class gets it right, because an item at that difficulty best discriminates students who understand from those who do not
It is asked at the very end of the lesson, because only then does it cover everything taught and show what needs reteaching
Each wrong option corresponds to a specific misconception, and the teacher can act on the result in the same lesson
It requires an extended written answer, because a short response cannot reveal the full reasoning a teacher needs to diagnose
diagnoses: Difficulty-calibration theory, borrowed from test design. A hinge exists to support a decision, not to spread scores; if nearly everyone is right, that is useful information too.
Timing error. A hinge sits at the fork in the lesson, mid-lesson, so the lesson can still change; an end-of-lesson check is an exit ticket, which informs tomorrow instead.
Correct. Diagnostic distractors tell you what to fix, and a response that can be read in about 30 seconds lets the lesson change while it is still happening.
Rigor equals length. Extended answers cannot be read for 30 students in real time, so they cannot drive a decision at the hinge point.

hinge.q: A school runs a two-day formative assessment workshop with a famous speaker. Nine months later, practice is unchanged. What is Wiliam and Leahy's most likely explanation?
options: The teachers are resistant to change, because a two-day workshop with a compelling speaker gives anyone willing all they need to start
Practice changes only through sustained, small, accountable steps with peer support; workshops transmit knowledge, not habits
The school needed a follow-up workshop, because a single event fades and a reinforcing message restores the momentum that was lost
The techniques do not work in this school's context, because if they had fitted, nine months would have been enough for teachers to keep them
diagnoses: Attribution to disposition. This is the fundamental attribution error applied to staff; Bryk would say the system that delivered the workshop produced the result.
Correct. Teaching is habitual real-time performance, and habit change needs repeated practice in one's own room with spaced follow-up, which is what the TLC structure provides.
More of the same. A second workshop repeats the delivery mechanism that failed; the missing ingredient is practice plus accountability over months.
Evidence-does-not-transfer. The techniques were never actually tried, so the context was never tested; nothing can be concluded about fit.

hinge.q: A new principal requires every teacher to use traffic-light cards daily and checks for them on walkthroughs. What is the most likely result?
options: Strong gains, because consistency across classrooms is what formative assessment needs and a mandate is the quickest route to getting it
Gains for younger students only, because traffic lights are a primary-school device that adolescents find patronizing and ignore
Teachers refuse outright, because a technique imposed by a new principal without consultation is rejected before it is ever tried
The cards appear in every room but teachers stop acting on the signals and students show green to avoid attention: a lethal mutation
diagnoses: Consistency of surface equals consistency of mechanism. The active ingredient is the teacher acting on the signal; a walkthrough can see the cards but not the adaptation.
Age-appropriateness theory. The problem is mutation under an evaluative mandate, not the age of the students.
Adoption-is-the-risk. Open refusal is rare; the realistic failure is quiet surface compliance, which is harder to detect.

Correct. This plan is tight on the technique and loose on the idea, the reverse of tight-but-loose. It produces compliance displays whose active ingredient is gone. Better: tight on the big idea and TLC process, with teacher choice of technique.

modules.title: The grammar of school and where deeper learning lives
modules.hook: Two researchers spent about six years and roughly 750 hours watching classes in 30 of America's most admired high schools, looking for deep learning. They found most of it in the same place in almost every school, and it was not the place the schools were built around. Where was it?

attempt.prompt: You must pick a 9th-grade schedule. Option A: eight 45-minute periods of conventional subjects. Option B: four 90-minute blocks, one of which is a daily interdisciplinary studio where students build projects for a public exhibition. Choose one and defend it in about 200 words. Then predict, concretely, the most likely way your choice goes wrong by February of year one, and who notices first.

objectives: Describe what Mehta & Fine actually observed (method, rarity of depth in the core, the periphery pattern) and the limits of that evidence.
Explain the four case schools' signature strengths and failures, and why the authors' ideal combines the progressive vision with the no-excuses operating system.
Apply the mastery, identity and creativity lens, and the six periphery features, to redesign a core course.
Use Transcend's blueprint (aims, then student experience, then elements) and say which layers are open to community codesign and which are bounded by evidence.

ideas.title: Deep learning is rare, and the grammar of school is part of why
ideas.body:
Jal Mehta (a Harvard sociologist) and Sarah Fine (a former English teacher) went looking for schools that had cracked **deeper learning**. They visited 30 high schools chosen for reputations for innovation or excellence, over about six years and roughly 750 hours of observation, shadowed students for whole days, interviewed students, teachers and leaders, and studied four schools in depth.

**Their definition is the most useful tool in the book.** Deeper learning is where three things happen together:
- **Mastery**: real understanding of a domain's knowledge and ways of reasoning.
- **Identity**: the learner starts to see the domain as part of who they are (*I am a writer*, *I do science*).
- **Creativity**: the learner moves from receiving the field to producing something within it.
Each alone is common. Mastery without identity gives students who can pass the exam and never open the subject again. Identity without mastery gives enthusiastic students who cannot do the work. Creativity without mastery gives products that look impressive and contain little.

**What they saw.** Even in schools selected *because* they were admired, most core classes were teacher talk, coverage, worksheets, recall questions, and students waiting for time to pass. Deep learning existed in pockets (a class here, a teacher there) in nearly every school and was almost never a property of the whole school. Shadowing whole days showed the student's experience to be fragmented: six or seven unrelated blocks, each with a different adult and different expectations, none requiring the student to own anything. Many students were compliant, bored, or strategically **doing school** (Denise Pope's term for performing grades without learning). Adults mostly did not know how the whole day felt. This matches decades of earlier observation research, such as Goodlad's *A Place Called School* (1984).

**The diagnosis: the grammar of schooling.** Tyack & Cuban (1995) named the durable, taken-for-granted structures of school: age-graded classes, subject silos, fixed periods, Carnegie units (credit for seat time), one teacher per room, grades as currency. On top sits a transmission model: students receive a field's conclusions but never practice the field, and teachers work alone with little shared picture of good work. Reforms that ignore the grammar get absorbed by it. Product analogy: the grammar is the platform. Ship a feature that fights the platform's defaults and it slowly gets reshaped into what the platform wanted all along.

**Two design consequences.** First, your structure (schedule, course grain size, how time and credit are counted) is itself a curriculum; it teaches students what school is for whether you intend it or not. Second, judge your school from the student's seat. Leaders shadowing a full student day, regularly, will see what showcase lessons and dashboards hide [H: well grounded descriptively; its effect on improvement is untested].

**Evidence limits you must carry.** This is qualitative, comparative case research: careful and theory-building, not causal. Schools were chosen for reputation, not sampled. Depth was judged by trained observers, not measured through learning outcomes or transfer, so we never learn whether one school's graduates understood more mathematics than another's. The mastery-identity-creativity lens is the authors' own; a researcher from the explicit-instruction tradition might score the same lessons differently. Tag the *description* (depth is rare in the core) as [E, observational]; tag the prescriptions as [H].

ideas.title: Every school model has a signature failure
ideas.body:
Mehta & Fine profile four schools under pseudonyms. Read them as four architectures, each with a known failure mode you should put in your risk register on day one.

**Dewey High (progressive, project-based; resembles High Tech High).** Strengths: interdisciplinary projects, public exhibitions, strong relationships, student voice, teachers designing their own curriculum; students felt known and liked school. Failure: quality varied enormously by teacher and project. Some projects were activity without learning; the widely cited example is students folding origami in maths who could not say what mathematics they were learning. Without explicit disciplinary goals and a shared, specific picture of excellent work, *project* became a container that could be full or empty. Radical teacher autonomy produced both the best and the weakest teaching, and there was no mechanism for spreading what the best teachers knew. Signature failure: **engagement without mastery**.

**No Excuses High (a high-performing charter).** Strengths: the most organizationally impressive school in the study. A coherent instructional model, frequent observation and feedback, data use, a shared adult culture, and staff who kept studying and refining practice; strong test results for low-income students of color. It was a powerful **learning organization for adults**. Failure: for students it was largely joyless and controlled; they were rarely treated as thinkers. It raised floors, not ceilings, and burnout and turnover were real costs. Signature failure: **compliance without agency**.

**IB High (International Baccalaureate).** The closest thing to a *system* for depth: an external curriculum, externally assessed tasks that demand analysis and sustained inquiry (Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge), shared vocabulary, and a global professional community. Because the assessments demand depth, teaching to them pulls toward depth, the opposite of most state tests. Failures: IB and non-IB students effectively attended different schools, and depth depended on teachers who understood the philosophy rather than treating IB as a heavier syllabus. Signature failure: **a two-tier school**.

**Attainment High (respected comprehensive).** Good conventional results, running on GPA, AP counts and admissions. Top-track students optimized for grades at the cost of curiosity and well-being; lower tracks got a thinner curriculum and lower expectations. Signature failure: **performance instead of learning**.

**The synthesis that matters.** What No Excuses High did well (shared instructional language, coaching, tight feedback loops, adult learning) is exactly what Dewey High lacked, and vice versa. The authors' implied ideal: **a rich vision of learning run on a disciplined adult operating system**. From IB, add the strongest lever they found: **alignment**. When curriculum, assessment and professional learning all reward depth, teaching bends toward depth; when assessment rewards recall, it bends toward recall. Their conditions for moving from pockets to systems: a clear shared vision of deep work, specific enough to guide practice; organizational capacity for adult learning; alignment; restructuring parts of the grammar; making the core more like the periphery; equity by design (no enclave); and leadership that protects depth from accountability pressure.

**Why this is tagged [H].** Each model is represented by one pseudonymous school. Reviewers (for instance in *Education Next*) argued the book gives no-excuses schools too little credit for measured gains among disadvantaged students. The four-way comparison is a vivid, plausible design vocabulary, not a verdict on the models. Use it to ask: whichever model you lean toward, what is its known failure, and what will you build on day one to prevent it?

ideas.title: The periphery out-teaches the core, so use it as the prototype
ideas.body:
The book's most cited finding: across the 30 schools, the most consistent sites of deep learning were **electives and extracurriculars**: theatre, debate, robotics, Model UN, the newspaper, music, athletics, some arts and technical courses. There students showed mastery, identity and creativity together, often in the same building where the core felt flat.

**Why the periphery works (six features)**
1. **Choice**: students opt in, which brings motivation and belonging.
2. **Purpose and real performance**: a game, a show, a competition, a publication, with a real audience and real stakes.
3. **Apprenticeship**: students do the actual activity of the field, not a school version of it, alongside adults who practice it.
4. **Community across ages**: older students coach younger ones; novices see what expertise looks like; there is a path from newcomer to leader (Lave & Wenger's legitimate peripheral participation).
5. **Time and iteration**: rehearsals and drafts, where failure is expected and useful.
6. **Identity**: students become *a debater* or *an actor*, not a student taking a course.
The core is required, coverage-driven, individually graded, age-segregated and detached from real practice; it reverses every one of these features. Schools treat the periphery as optional and cut it first, yet it is where the learning they claim to want most often happens.

**The caveats are large.** Students who choose debate were already motivated (selection). The periphery faces no state test and has smaller, self-selected groups, so the comparison is not like for like. Voluntariness is hard to transplant into a required course. And, crucially for this curriculum, **the periphery is full of explicit instruction**. Coaches drill, directors model, editors mark up drafts line by line. Kirschner, Sweller & Clark's warning against minimal guidance for novices is not contradicted here; the periphery works partly because it is highly guided. *Authentic* means authentic purpose and audience, not absence of teaching. Brown, Collins & Duguid's situated-cognition claims were likewise criticized by Anderson, Reder & Simon (1996) as overstated; the reconciliation is cognitive apprenticeship: explicit modelling and scaffolding toward authentic practice.

**Deeper teaching in the core.** A minority of core teachers, in every type of school, produced depth. They shared a **disciplinary stance** (the subject as a living field of inquiry, not a topic list), treated students as apprentice practitioners, combined **rigor with joy**, used apprenticeship moves (model, scaffold, hand over), and covered fewer topics more deeply. Most had built that capacity outside or despite their school: graduate study, writing projects, earlier careers. Hence the **symmetry principle**: teachers need the conditions the school wants for students (mastery, identity, creativity, community). Teachers who never learned deeply in a field struggle to create depth for others.

**The design move.** Treat the periphery as the prototype for the core, not a reward for finishing it. Ask of every core course: What is the performance? Who is the audience? Who is the more expert practitioner? How does a novice become a leader? Where does student choice enter? Then keep what makes the core the core: a knowledge sequence, explicit teaching for novices, and mastery checks. Do not solve this by adding a studio block and leaving the core alone; that recreates the finding inside your own timetable, with the depth in the new block and the core still shallow.

**Tag honestly.** The periphery pattern is a strong, recurring description [E, observational, selection-confounded]; importing its features into required courses is a hypothesis [H] you will test.

ideas.title: Designing with a community: aims, experience, elements, and where voice is bounded
ideas.body:
Mehta & Fine show what is wrong with the student experience. Samouha, Wetzler & Henry Wood (Transcend) offer a process for designing a better one *with* the people who will live in it. Read it as product development for schools, including the parts of product development that go wrong.

**The target.** **Graduate Aims** in three areas, synthesized from more than 30 outcome frameworks: **intellectual prowess** (deep knowledge and the ability to use it), **wayfinding** (purpose, identity, self-direction, career and life navigation), and **well-being**. Then ten **Leaps**, shifts in the *student experience* from industrial-era patterns: for example rote activity to rigorous learning, irrelevance to relevance, isolation to connection, passive compliance to active self-direction, unequal expectations to high expectations with unlimited opportunities. The Leaps are a design language, not a model; a community prioritizes a few rather than claiming all ten (nobody makes every leap at once; two to four is a sensible start). Transcend's Leaps Student Voice Survey, with published psychometric reports, turns them into a leading indicator you can track each term.

**The blueprint has three layers, designed top-down**: (1) aims and guiding concepts; (2) the **student experience**, meaning what a day, week and year actually feel like; (3) the **elements**: schedule, staffing, curriculum, assessment, culture, space, technology, partnerships, budget, policy. The classic failure is designing elements first (a device rollout, a new bell schedule) with no stated experience they are meant to produce. That is shipping infrastructure without a user story.

**The process.** A diverse **design team** including students and families, deliberately recruiting the least-served voices. A repeating design cycle, used as **Map It** (whole-school vision), **Zoom In** (design one part of the experience in detail), **Test-Drive** (pilot with success measures set in advance), **Look Ahead** (keep, change or drop), then scale, re-map and routine maintenance. Tend **community conditions** (trust, urgency, shared vision, capacity) as deliberately as the design, because a technically good design the community does not own gets quietly reverted. **Codify** what works: Van Ness Elementary's whole-child routines spread to other schools because they were written down as teachable practice. Northern Cass shows the deepest structural change (competency-based progression, no letter grades) and how much work it pushes into transcripts, reporting and teacher workload. Map your **policy envelope** (seat-time rules, testing, credits, accreditation) early.

**Evidence limits.** A practitioner framework by the organization that sells the process. There is no causal evaluation of community-based design. The four cases are selected success stories with uncontrolled outcomes. Transcend's large *Beyond Fine* analysis links better-reported experience to grades, test scores and attendance, but it is correlational and self-published. Competency-based education has a thin, mixed causal record. Several Leaps are value commitments, and *active self-direction* and *anytime, anywhere learning* are in real tension with the novice-guidance evidence.

**The rule that makes it safe.** Community voice is excellent at defining **needs and priorities** and poor at validating **mechanisms**. If a focus group asks for teaching matched to learning styles, take the underlying need seriously (*instruction doesn't fit my child*) and answer it with evidence-based customization such as pace, formative feedback and choice of context, not with a debunked mechanism. Standardize the mechanisms (retrieval, feedback, TLCs, the default lesson, the knowledge sequence within a discipline). Codesign purpose, culture, the periphery, and knowledge priorities where the evidence is silent. Write down which layer is open, in the founding compact, before the first session.

worked_example.title: Decision: how does the school bring apprenticeship into the core, not just the periphery?
steps: Name the features that make the periphery work: choice, real purpose and audience, apprenticeship to a practitioner, mixed-age community, iteration, identity. [E, observational and selection-confounded]
Reject the tempting design: adding a studio block and leaving the core untouched. That reproduces Mehta & Fine's finding inside your own timetable: depth in the new block, shallow core. [H]

Redesign each core disciplinary course so every unit or term ends in a product with a real audience (a published piece, a public problem-solving defense, a data report for a local body), drafts are expected and critiqued, and the teacher's own disciplinary practice is visible. [H]

Keep the knowledge sequence and explicit teaching. The product is the destination of a knowledge-building unit, not a replacement for it; the periphery itself is heavily coached, and novices still need guidance (Kirschner, Sweller & Clark). [E for novice guidance; H for the combination]

Guard against Dewey High's failure: each product has explicit disciplinary learning goals, annotated exemplars and a critique protocol, and the maths or science in it is checked by a hinge question or short assessment, not inferred from how good the poster looks. [H, informed by E from Module 6]

Borrow No Excuses High's operating system without its theory of learning: shared instructional language, frequent developmental observation, common planning, and TLCs, pointed at the richer vision. Track joy and agency as outcomes, or control-heavy routines will quietly optimize them away. [H; V for tracking joy]

On structure there is a real tension. Mehta & Fine recommend restructuring parts of the grammar (longer blocks, fewer topics); Wiliam's evidence says structural change alone buys little and eats change capacity. Resolution: keep the schedule mostly conventional in year one, lengthen blocks only where a specific instructional need requires it (for example, lab or studio work), and test that change as an explicit hypothesis. [H]
Hire and develop teachers who have done the discipline, not only taught it, and give them adult learning with its own depth (symmetry). [H]
Protect and fund the periphery anyway, with mixed-age leadership ladders and access for every student. It is where identity lives. [V]
Policy line for the brief: Every core course, every term, one authentic product, built on a knowledge sequence, and assessed for mastery.

hinge.q: According to Mehta & Fine, the main reason electives and clubs often show deeper learning than core classes is:
options: They have smaller groups, and with fewer students each one gets the individual attention that produces depth in any setting
They combine real purpose and audience, apprenticeship to practitioners, mixed-age community and iteration, as well as choice
Students choose them, and choosing an activity supplies the motivation that required classes cannot, whatever their design
They are not tested, and removing the exam pressure lets teachers and students pursue a topic as deeply as it deserves
diagnoses: Resource explanation. Group size differs, but Module 8 shows class size alone has modest effects; the features that matter are about the nature of the work.
Correct. The periphery bundles several structural features the core reverses; choice is one of six, alongside purpose, apprenticeship, community, iteration and identity.
Choice-only theory. Choice is one of the features, and selection is a real confound, but it cannot explain why the same students go flat in required courses that lack the other features.
Testing-kills-learning theory. The lack of test pressure is an acknowledged confound, but IB High shows that assessment demanding depth can pull teaching toward depth.

hinge.q: A founder plans a project-based school with no traditional courses. Mehta & Fine's evidence suggests the most likely failure mode is:
options: Students will be bored, because projects lack the pace and variety of a timetable and long tasks lose adolescents' attention
Teachers will refuse to teach that way, because most were trained in courses and resist a model that sidelines their subject expertise
Parents will withdraw their children, because families judge schools by recognizable courses and grades and distrust project work
Disciplinary mastery will be uneven, and some projects will be activity without learning, depending on which teacher a student gets
diagnoses: Engagement-is-the-risk. Dewey High's students were engaged and liked school; engagement was not the problem.
Adoption-is-the-risk. Teachers at Dewey High chose it and embraced the model; autonomy produced variance, not refusal.
Market-is-the-risk. Possible, but not what the observational evidence speaks to; the evidence is about uneven rigor.

Correct. This is Dewey High's signature failure (the origami-in-maths problem): without explicit disciplinary goals, exemplars and a system to spread good designs, quality depends on which teacher you get.

hinge.q: Deeper learning in Mehta & Fine's sense requires:
options: Mastery, identity and creativity together, because each alone is common and only their combination marks the richest learning
A technology-rich environment, because real tools let students produce work of a kind that textbook exercises cannot reach
Student choice of topic, because a learner who has chosen the subject invests the sustained attention that depth requires
Interdisciplinary content, because a problem seen through several subjects at once cannot be handled at a surface level
diagnoses: Correct. Each alone is common; their combination is what the authors observed in the richest learning, and it gives you a test to apply to any course.
Tools equal depth. Nothing in the definition concerns technology; Module 1's point that medium is not mechanism applies here too.
Choice equals depth. Choice can support identity, but a freely chosen shallow project is still shallow.
Integration equals depth. Interdisciplinary units can be as shallow as any other; depth is about the learner's relationship to a field.

hinge.q: Which conclusion does Mehta & Fine's evidence actually support?
options: Longer blocks produce deeper learning, since every school where the authors found depth had abandoned the 50-minute period
Project-based schools produce better learning outcomes than no-excuses schools, since depth appeared in the former and not the latter
Deep learning was rare in the core classes even of admired schools and recurred in the periphery; a robust pattern, not causal proof
Extracurriculars cause deeper learning, so required academics should be replaced with clubs, since the same students flourish there
diagnoses: Structure-as-solution. Longer blocks are one of the authors' proposals, not a finding; Wiliam's evidence cautions that structure alone changes little.
Outcome claim the study cannot make. There were no learning-outcome measures and one school per model; the authors praise No Excuses High's adult systems.
Correct. The strength of the book is descriptive: a recurring pattern across 30 reputationally selected schools. The prescriptions are well-grounded hypotheses.
Correlation-as-causation plus misreading the prescription. The evidence is selection-confounded, and the authors want the core made more like the periphery, keeping mastery, not academics abolished.

hinge.q: Your founding design team's family focus groups strongly favor teaching students in their preferred learning style. Using Transcend's process as this module bounds it, you should:
options: Put it to a vote of the whole community, because a contested question about teaching is settled most legitimately by the people whose children it affects most directly
Treat it as evidence of a real need (instruction does not fit some children) and meet it with evidence-based customization of pace, feedback and context
Ignore it, because community input should not touch pedagogy and families who choose the school are choosing its expertise over their own instincts
Adopt it, because community ownership is a design requirement and a school that overrides its families loses the coalition it needs to open and survive
diagnoses: Majority-rule-on-mechanism. Voting settles values questions, not empirical ones.
Correct. Voice defines needs and priorities; evidence constrains mechanisms. The founding compact should say which layer is open to codesign.
Voice-is-noise. This discards a real signal and damages the community conditions the design depends on; the need is legitimate even though the proposed mechanism is wrong.
Voice-validates-mechanism. Ownership matters, but communities can converge on popular, ineffective ideas; learning-styles matching is not supported by evidence.

modules.brief_prompt: Rewrite the 16-year-old's Tuesday in Section 2 of your brief so that at least one core course shows apprenticeship features (a real product, an audience, drafts, a practitioner-teacher), and note what you deliberately kept conventional and why. In Section 1, draft Graduate Aims across intellectual prowess, wayfinding and well-being, and pick two to four priority experience shifts. Add a paragraph on community codesign that names which layers are open (purpose, culture, periphery, knowledge priorities where evidence is silent) and which are fixed by evidence (core mechanisms), tagged V and H. Add to your risk register the signature failure of whichever model your school most resembles, and the day-one countermeasure.
