modules.title: What actually moves outcomes: teachers, policy, and the evidence
modules.hook: Wiliam's rough summary of the research: with the most effective teachers, students learn in about half the usual time; with the least effective, it takes about twice as long. If teachers matter that much, why does he argue that trying to hire your way to a great faculty barely moves the average?

attempt.prompt: You have $600k a year of discretionary budget for a 400-student school. Options: (1) cut class sizes from 26 to 22; (2) hire an instructional coach for each department; (3) buy 1:1 devices plus adaptive maths and reading software; (4) raise salaries 8% to attract stronger applicants; (5) anything else you can name. Allocate the money and justify each line in one or two sentences. Then write down the one number you would most want to know before committing, and why.

objectives: Evaluate any initiative on five criteria: effect on learning, cost in money and teacher time, scalability, opportunity cost, and time to impact.
Explain why teacher quality is the biggest in-school lever, yet selection, deselection and incentive pay are weak ways to raise it.
Rank the common structural reforms (class size, choice, copying other countries) by evidence and cost, and explain the ranking.
Read an effect size and name its main traps: student age, test proximity, sample restriction, and scale-up decay.
State Wiliam's two priorities (knowledge-rich curriculum; developing existing teachers through formative assessment in TLCs) and defend them on cost-effectiveness.

ideas.title: Think like a portfolio manager: benefit per unit of scarce resource
ideas.body:
*Creating the Schools Our Children Need* is the curriculum's resource-allocation book. Wiliam's starting point: education does not lack good ideas; it has too many good-sounding ideas competing for the same limited money, teacher hours and leadership attention. So the question is never *does it work?* (almost everything works a little, somewhere) but **is this the best use of what it consumes?**

**Five criteria for every initiative**
1. **Effect** on student learning, ideally expressed in months of learning for your students' age, not a raw effect size.
2. **Cost**, in dollars *and* teacher hours. A free app that consumes three hours of teacher training and a weekly data meeting is not free.
3. **Scalability**: does it work in ordinary schools with ordinary teachers, without the enthusiasts who designed it?
4. **Opportunity cost**: what it pushes out of a full week. Every hour of meetings is an hour not planning, marking or resting.
5. **Time to impact**: a decade-long lever is a different bet from a one-year one.

**"Everything works somewhere, nothing works everywhere."** Context changes the effect. Research cannot tell you exactly what to do; it can tell you which bets have the best odds. This is the same point Bryk makes as *what works, for whom, under what conditions* (Module 9). Borrow **mechanisms** that have causal evidence and test them locally; do not copy **policies** because they are attached to a famous school or country.

**The binding constraint is usually teacher time, not money.** Wiliam's hardest leadership lesson: the job is **stopping things**, de-implementing good-but-not-best initiatives so the best ones get done properly. Initiative overload is the default failure mode of schools, and it maps precisely onto Module 1: a staff with too many simultaneous initiatives is a working memory with too many interacting elements. Nothing gets encoded.

**Product translation.** You already know this pattern as prioritization by expected value per unit cost, with a roadmap that has a *not doing* list. Two differences matter. First, the variance is larger than in most product work, and your sample is tiny (one school), so humility about local effects is warranted. Second, the cost of a failed bet is paid in children's learning time, which you cannot refund, so the bar for untested structural bets should be higher, not lower.

**Design rules for your founding document** [H for all; the logic is strong, but evidence on de-implementation itself is thinner than the argument for it]:
- Name **two or three priorities** and publish a **not doing** list.
- Every new proposal must name what it replaces, its expected effect in months, and its cost in teacher hours.
- Budget teacher time explicitly, like money: hours per teacher per month for professional learning, planning and meetings.
- Commit to a three-to-five-year horizon on the core priorities. Changing initiatives every year guarantees none of them embed.

**Folk theory to retire:** a new school, free of legacy, should try many innovations at once because it can. Autonomy lets you choose well; it does not repeal the time budget.

ideas.title: Teachers matter most, and you cannot select your way there
ideas.body:
The premise is not in dispute. Teacher quality is the largest in-school variable, and differences between classrooms in the same school dwarf differences between schools. Wiliam's summary (a rhetorical rounding of value-added research; exact multipliers vary by study): with the best teachers students learn in roughly half the time; with the weakest, about twice as long.

The surprise is what follows. Three popular ways to raise teacher quality are weak.

**1. Hiring smarter people.** What you can see at hiring (degrees, certification, college selectivity, licensure scores, even subject-knowledge tests) predicts later effectiveness only weakly. Kane, Rockoff & Staiger (2008), in New York City, found certified, uncertified and alternatively certified teachers differed little on average, while variation *within* each group was huge. Teach For America evaluations show small positive effects in some subjects, not transformation. Raising entry bars also reduces supply, and in shortage subjects a higher bar can mean more vacancies filled by substitutes.

**2. Firing weak teachers (deselection).** Hanushek estimated that replacing the bottom 5-10% of US teachers with average ones would bring national achievement near the top countries. The arithmetic works; the practice does not. **Measurement**: value-added estimates are noisy, with year-to-year correlations for the same teacher of roughly 0.2-0.5, so many teachers in the bottom group one year are not the next. The Gates MET project (2010-2013) showed classroom observation is unreliable unless you use multiple trained observers across multiple lessons. **Time**: deselection improves the workforce only as cohorts turn over, over a decade or more. **Supply**: replacements are often novices, who are on average less effective in their first years. **Climate**: a threat culture discourages risk-taking and collaboration and drives good people away. Removing a truly ineffective teacher is sometimes necessary: HR hygiene, not an improvement strategy.

**3. Paying good teachers more.** Individual merit pay relies on that same unreliable measurement and can damage collaboration. The Nashville POINT trial (Springer et al. 2010; bonuses up to $15,000) found no significant effect; Fryer's NYC school-wide bonus study (2013) found none either. A loss-framed design in Chicago Heights (Fryer, Levitt, List & Sadoff 2012) did show effects, but that is thin evidence and hard to scale. The underlying point: most teachers already work hard. The bottleneck is knowing *how* to improve, not motivation. Pay competitively and fairly for recruitment and retention [V/H], but do not expect incentive pay to raise teaching quality [E].

**What this means for a founder.** You cannot select your way to a great faculty, so design to **develop** whoever you hire. Teachers improve a great deal in their first few years (Rockoff 2004), and growth continues longer in supportive professional environments (Kraft & Papay 2014). A school where teachers visibly get better is also a retention strategy. Hire for disciplinary knowledge and **coachability**, and test both with job-relevant work samples (teach a short lesson, take feedback, reteach; respond to real student work) rather than trusting credentials or a single polished demo [H: plausible, test it in your own hiring]. Never base high-stakes decisions on single-year value-added or single observations [E].

ideas.title: Structural reforms change the container, not the contents
ideas.body:
The second half of Wiliam's list of reforms that will not help much is structural. Each has real evidence behind it. The point is not that it does nothing; it is that it does too little for what it costs, or does not survive scale.

**Class size.** Tennessee STAR (1985-89) is one of the best randomized trials in education: K-3 classes of about 13-17 versus 22-25 produced gains of roughly 0.15-0.2 SD, larger for Black and low-income students. So small classes help, especially early. Then California reduced class sizes statewide in 1996 and got much smaller gains (Jepsen & Rivkin 2009). Scaling required hiring huge numbers of new, often uncertified teachers; stronger teachers moved to more advantaged schools; space ran out. The loss in teacher quality ate much of the benefit. Class-size reduction is also the most expensive recurring cost you can choose, because salaries are the biggest budget line, and it is hard to reverse. Founder rules: do not make small classes your main value proposition or spend on them before teacher learning [E]; targeted small groups for early reading or catch-up may capture much of the benefit at a fraction of the cost [H]; and if parents value small classes for being known and cared for, that is a legitimate value, so name it honestly as [V].

**Copying other countries.** PISA and TIMSS show what is possible, but features of Finland, Singapore or Shanghai are tangled with culture, teacher status, demographics, private tutoring and social policy. A system can succeed despite a policy, not because of it, and many policy mixes produce high scores. Borrow mechanisms with causal evidence (for example, collaborative teacher inquiry of the lesson-study kind, adapted as a principle), not policies.

**School choice and charters.** CREDO's national studies found average charter effects near zero with **very wide variation**; lottery studies of Boston charters and KIPP found large positive effects; some voucher programs (Louisiana, around 2013-15) showed negative first-year maths effects. Because variation *between* schools is small compared with variation *within* them, reshuffling students among schools has a limited ceiling. The charters that succeed do so because of what happens inside classrooms: curriculum, instruction, culture, teacher development.

**The sentence to write on your wall: being a new or independent school confers no advantage by itself.** Autonomy is only an asset if you spend it on the classroom-level levers. Every founder is tempted to believe the new container is the innovation. It is not. The contents are.

**How this connects.** Mehta & Fine (Module 7) reached a compatible conclusion from observation: models, governance and structure did not reliably produce depth; adult learning and alignment did. Bryk (Module 9) explains the mechanism: structural reforms change one part of a complex system and assume the rest adjusts, which is why the same reform works in some places, fails in others, and averages out small.

**Evidence strength.** STAR, CREDO and the lottery studies are strong. The comparative claim that teacher development beats class size per dollar is Wiliam's reasoned estimate from separate literatures, not a head-to-head trial [H for the ranking; E for the components]. Critics also note a possible double standard: the author's own field, formative assessment, gets a gentler reading. His case survives the smaller at-scale estimates (about 0.1 SD) on cost, but not his early doubling-the-speed rhetoric.

ideas.title: Reading effect sizes without getting fooled
ideas.body:
An effect size (standardized mean difference) is the gap between two groups measured in standard deviations. It looks like a universal currency, which is exactly why it misleads. Vendors, consultants and league tables (Hattie's ranking is the famous one) compare numbers that cannot be compared. Four traps catch almost everyone.

**1. Age.** Young children learn fast relative to the spread of scores; teenagers learn slowly relative to it. A year of normal growth is a large effect in the early grades and roughly 0.25-0.4 SD at secondary (Bloom, Hill, Black & Lipsey 2008). So an effect of 0.2 can mean a few weeks of extra learning for a 7-year-old and most of a year for a 15-year-old. **Translate effect sizes into months of learning for the age in question** before comparing anything.

**2. The test.** A researcher-designed test closely aligned to what the intervention taught produces much bigger effects than a broad standardized test of the same subject. A narrow test measures whether students learned the taught content; a broad one measures whether it moved the general achievement you care about. Both are legitimate, but they are not the same number.

**3. The sample.** Studying a restricted group (only struggling readers, only one ability band) shrinks the standard deviation and inflates the effect size. Timing matters too: a measure taken a week after the intervention flatters; one taken a year later tells you what lasted (Module 4's point that short-term performance lies).

**4. Scale-up decay.** Small studies run by enthusiastic designers produce larger effects than the same idea run by ordinary teachers across many schools. Formative assessment is this module's own case study: roughly 0.4-0.7 in the 1998 review, about 0.3 in KMOFAP, about 0.1 in the 140-school EEF trial. Nothing failed. That is what scale does.

**A practical reading protocol** for any claim that crosses your desk (a vendor deck, a board member's article, an AI tutoring pilot):
- Who were the students (age, prior attainment), and how does that compare with yours?
- What test, and who designed it? How long after the intervention?
- Randomized, or a before-after comparison with no control?
- Who delivered it: the designers, or ordinary staff?
- What did it cost, including teacher time, and what would it displace?
- Has it been replicated at scale, and what happened to the effect?

**Worked contrast.** Two interventions each report 0.4. One was measured on 7-year-olds, with a researcher-built test, a week later. The other on 15-year-olds, with a standardized test, a year later. The second is far more impressive: older students, a broad test and a delayed measure all *deflate* effect sizes, so the same number represents a much larger real change.

**Why a founder must own this skill.** Every week someone will offer you a number. Kraft (2020) and Simpson (2017) extended the critique of comparing effect sizes. The discipline is not cynicism; Wiliam's own recommendations are built on effect sizes, read carefully. It is the education version of refusing to compare conversion rates across different funnels, segments and time windows.

ideas.title: The two bets: a knowledge-rich curriculum and developing the teachers you have
ideas.body:
Having ruled out the popular levers, Wiliam names two priorities. Almost everything else is lower.

**Bet 1: curriculum.** Content and its sequence, and the materials teachers use, are a major and under-used lever, and cheap, because schools buy materials anyway. Randomized comparisons of elementary maths curricula (Agodini et al. 2010) and the Brookings analysis *Choosing Blindly* (Chingos & Whitehurst 2012) suggest that choosing between textbooks can produce differences comparable to expensive reforms at near-zero marginal cost. Distinguish the **intended** curriculum (specified), the **enacted** curriculum (taught) and the **achieved** curriculum (learned); improvement lives in the gaps between them. Adopting a curriculum does not mean it is being taught, which is Wexler's warning in Module 5.

Why *knowledge-rich*? Module 1's architecture: working memory is tiny, long-term memory is vast, and expertise is organized knowledge that frees working memory for thinking. Critical thinking, problem solving and creativity are not generic skills that transfer without content. Reading comprehension, once decoding is fluent, depends heavily on topic knowledge (Recht & Leslie 1988: weak readers who knew baseball out-comprehended strong readers who did not, on a baseball passage). And it is an **equity** lever: advantaged children pick up background knowledge at home, so a school that does not teach it systematically widens gaps. Protect elementary time for science, history, geography and the arts as knowledge-building, not only literacy and numeracy skills blocks. *Which* knowledge is a value choice [V], so make it explicitly with your community. Causal evidence for whole curricula is growing (a Core Knowledge charter lottery study, Grissmer et al. 2023, postdates the book); in 2018 Wiliam argued mainly from mechanism.

**Bet 2: improve the teachers you already have.** Wiliam calls it *love the one you're with*. Most professional development as delivered (one-off workshops, generic inspiration) shows little measurable effect; TNTP's *The Mirage* (2015) found high spending and hard-to-detect results. The **content** of development should be classroom formative assessment, because it applies across subjects and ages, works on the short cycle, and has meaningful effects at low cost. The **process** should be TLCs: monthly, multi-year, teacher-chosen techniques, small steps, peer accountability (Module 6). Evidence published around or after the book strengthens the case: the EEF trial (about two months' extra progress across 140 schools) and syntheses of PD mechanisms such as Sims et al. (2021), which favor sustained, practice-focused designs. The exact TLC parameters remain sensible defaults, not proven optima.

**Why these two together.** Shared, school-wide materials make teacher collaboration far more productive, because everyone is improving the same lessons. Formative assessment without a good curriculum adapts toward nothing; a good curriculum without formative assessment is taught to the imagined median student.

**What the two bets leave out.** Wiliam has little on motivation, well-being, culture or curiosity, so use Yeager, Engel and Mehta & Fine as counterweights. He is also readier than Bryk to name the answer in advance: his is the *what*, Bryk's the *how*. The founder's synthesis: **pick the best-odds bets from the evidence, then use improvement science to make them work in your building.**

**Staffing consequence.** Select for learnability; build for effectiveness. Invest heavily in years one to three of every teacher's time with you; make TLC participation part of the employment compact [V]; and apply the mentor mindset to adults too: high standards, high support, transparency about why.

worked_example.title: Decision: hiring versus development, and the $600k allocation
steps: Restate the problem in Wiliam's terms: not which options work (all of them do a little) but which yields the most learning per dollar and per teacher-hour for our students, what each displaces, and how fast it pays off. [H for the rubric; it is a decision framework]
Pre-hire signals (credentials, interviews, even a single demo lesson) predict effectiveness weakly, and value-added and single observations are noisy. So hiring cannot carry the strategy. [E]
Variation among teachers already in the building is large, and teachers improve substantially in their early years, longer in supportive environments. The reachable lever is development. [E]

Salary +8%: helps recruitment and retention over years, but spreads thin, recurs forever, and merit-style pay has null trial results. Keep pay competitive and fair; do not buy quality with it. Allocate a modest amount to fair pay, framed as a retention and values decision. [E on merit pay; V on fairness]

Class size 26 to 22: real but modest effects, strongest in early grades, the largest recurring cost, and it forces extra hires. Reject school-wide; fund targeted small-group early-reading intervention instead. [E for the pattern; H for the targeted alternative]

Devices plus adaptive software: medium is not mechanism (Module 1). Fund only a specific mechanism with a plausible effect for our age group, such as spaced retrieval practice, piloted as a PDSA with a practical measure, not a 1:1 rollout. [E that technology does not teach by itself; H for the pilot]

Coaches: fund, but pointed at formative assessment and the curriculum, working through TLCs rather than as freelance experts. Add protected TLC time (the real cost is teacher hours, so cancel a meeting to pay for it) and high-quality shared curriculum materials. [E for sustained, practice-focused PD and curriculum; H for the exact split]

Hire for disciplinary depth and coachability, tested with a teach-take-feedback-reteach work sample; make TLC participation a condition of employment; make years one to three a structured development program. [H for the criteria; V for the compact]
Write the prediction: about 0.1 SD whole-school over two years from the TLC and formative work, measured externally, with leading indicators reviewed termly. [E for the magnitude]
Policy line for the brief: We select for learnability and build for effectiveness; every new initiative names what it replaces.

hinge.q: Wiliam's main argument against building a strategy on firing weak teachers and hiring stronger ones is:
options: It is unkind to teachers, because a profession built on trust cannot survive a strategy that treats its members as replaceable parts
Teachers are all roughly equally effective, because once training and experience are equal the differences between them are small
Our measures of teacher quality are too noisy before and after hiring, replacements are often novices, and change comes too slowly
Unions make it impossible, because tenure protections and grievance procedures mean the weakest teachers can rarely be removed
diagnoses: Values reading of an evidence argument. Wiliam may also hold that value, but his case rests on measurement reliability, supply and time.
Reverses the premise. Variation among teachers is large; that is the whole reason teacher quality is the key lever.
Correct. Credentials predict weakly, value-added correlates only about 0.2-0.5 year to year, deselection improves the workforce only as cohorts turn over, and replacements start less effective.
Political-constraint reading. Even with no political barriers, the measurement and supply problems remain.

hinge.q: Two interventions both report an effect size of 0.4. One was measured on 7-year-olds with a researcher-designed test one week later; the other on 15-year-olds with a standardized test one year later. Which is more impressive?
options: The second, because older students, a broad standardized test and a year's delay all deflate effect sizes, so 0.4 there means more
Neither, because 0.4 is 0.4: an effect size standardizes the gain so that studies with different tests and ages can be compared
The first, because 0.4 is a large effect for young children, whose scores are hard to move before basic skills are in place
The first, because a shorter delay gives a cleaner measurement, uncontaminated by everything else that happens over a year
diagnoses: Correct. Older students, a broad standardized test and a delayed measure all deflate effect sizes, so 0.4 under those conditions represents a much larger real change.
Effect sizes as universal currency. They depend on age, test and sample; comparing them raw is the league-table error.
Reverses the age effect. Young children grow fast relative to the score spread, so effect sizes are naturally larger for them; 0.4 means less for a 7-year-old.
Proximity equals validity. A test right after the intervention on its own content measures short-term performance, which flatters; a delayed broad test shows what lasted.

hinge.q: According to Wiliam, the best-evidenced use of a marginal dollar of school improvement money is:
options: Performance pay, because teachers who are rewarded for results direct their effort where it counts and the weakest are pushed to improve or leave
Technology, because well-designed adaptive software gives each student the individualized pace and feedback no teacher can provide
Reducing class size, because every student gets more of the teacher's attention and the effect is proven by a large randomized trial
Sustained, school-based teacher development in classroom formative assessment, alongside a strong curriculum, because it reaches every room
diagnoses: Incentive theory. Randomized US merit-pay trials mostly found no effect; teachers' bottleneck is know-how, not effort.
Modernity theory. Technology does not teach by itself; it helps only when it delivers a specific mechanism.
Intuitive and popular. Real but modest effects at very high recurring cost, diluted at scale (STAR versus California).
Correct. It reaches every classroom, is cheap relative to structural change, and has trial evidence at scale (about two months' progress), with curriculum as the cheap complementary lever.

hinge.q: Tennessee STAR found meaningful gains from small classes. California's statewide class-size reduction produced much smaller gains. The best explanation is:
options: Small classes only work in Tennessee, because every intervention depends on context and effects found in one place rarely travel
Scaling required mass hiring of less experienced and often uncertified teachers, which offset much of the benefit of smaller classes
California's students were harder to teach, because a more diverse and mobile population responds less to changes in class size
STAR was a flawed study, because a single state's experiment with volunteer schools could not show what a real policy would do
diagnoses: Context-mysticism. Everything works somewhere does not mean effects are arbitrary; here the mechanism of the failure is known.
Correct. This is scale-up decay with a named mechanism: the reform consumed the very resource (good teachers) that makes classes effective, and moved strong teachers toward advantaged schools.
Population-difference guess. Student mix may matter at the margin, but the documented mechanism is the change in teacher quality.
Dismissing strong evidence. STAR was a large randomized trial and is among the most credible studies in education.

hinge.q: A co-founder says: our charter status and freedom from district rules will make us better than local schools. The best response from this module is:
options: It depends entirely on funding, because autonomy without the money to use it changes nothing, and with it any structure would work
Agreed, because lottery studies of charter schools show large gains, and freedom from district rules is what lets those schools achieve them at scale
Structure confers no advantage by itself; choice schools show small average effects with wide variation, and the good ones win inside classrooms
Wrong, because charters perform worse on average, and the freedom from rules that founders prize is what lets standards slip unnoticed
diagnoses: Resource reductionism. Funding matters at the margin, but the evidence points to what happens inside classrooms as the differentiator.
Cherry-picking the tail. Some urban networks show large lottery-based gains; national averages are near zero. Your school is not automatically in the good tail.
Correct. Autonomy is an option, not an asset; it pays only if spent on curriculum, instruction, culture and teacher development.
Overcorrection. Averages are near zero with wide spread, not reliably negative.

modules.brief_prompt: Add or rewrite Section 7 (Adults) of your brief: hiring criteria and the work-sample you will use, the first-three-years development plan, and the TLC compact. Add a budget table allocating the $600k (or your own discretionary figure) with, for each line, the expected effect in months of learning, the cost in dollars and teacher hours, and what it displaces. Add a one-paragraph initiative-evaluation rubric and a first not-doing list of at least three things. Tag every line E/H/V, and flag any claim that rests on a raw effect size you have not translated for age and test type.

modules.title: Running the school as an improvement system
modules.hook: Suppose your new advisory program lifts average attendance. Then someone breaks the data out and finds it helps most students, does nothing for many, and makes things worse for a small group who were already the most at risk. Your board wants to roll it out to every grade. What is the first question improvement science asks, and why is 'did it work on average?' the wrong one?

attempt.prompt: Your school's Year 7 maths attainment has been flat for two years. In 15 minutes: (1) sketch the system that produces this result: the people, processes, handoffs and routines, not just the causes you suspect; (2) name three things (drivers) you believe must change; (3) write the first two-week test of one change, including exactly what you will do, with whom, what you predict will happen, and how you will measure it by Friday of week two. Do it before reading on.

objectives: Explain why variation in performance, not the average effect, is the central object of improvement, and apply 'see the system' to a school outcome.
Draw a driver diagram (aim, primary drivers, secondary drivers, change ideas) with a measure at each level.
Design a PDSA cycle with a written prediction, a practical measure and a balancing measure, and explain why it is not an A/B test.
Distinguish measurement for accountability, research and improvement, and say what each does to behavior.
Judge where the software analogies (incident review, observability, canary releases) hold and where they break, and state the evidence limits of Bryk's cases.

ideas.title: The system produces the result: study variation, not averages
ideas.body:
Anthony Bryk ran the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching from 2008 to 2020. *Improvement in Action* (2020) is a casebook; the method comes from its predecessor, *Learning to Improve* (Bryk, Gomez, Grunow & LeMahieu 2015). The diagnosis first, because it is the best-evidenced part.

**Why reform keeps failing.** American reform runs a loop: adopt a big solution, roll it out everywhere, get widely varying results that are mediocre on average, give up, adopt the next big solution. Schools are complex systems: schedules, roles, curricula, data, norms and relationships jointly produce outcomes. Reforms change one part and assume the rest will adjust. It does not, so the same intervention works here, fails there, and averages out to *small effect*. Most reforms fail in **implementation**, not in their ideas. Decades of implementation research (the RAND Change Agent studies onward) support this. Hence Bryk's reframe: not *what works?* but **what works, for whom, under what conditions?** A randomized trial gives you an average; a leader needs to know whether it will work *here* and what to adjust.

**Principle: focus on variation in performance.** Variation is where the information is. Look at the tails: classrooms, teachers or students where things go unusually well (**positive deviants**, often your best source of change ideas) or badly. The goal is **quality reliably at scale**: shrinking the bad tail, not just raising the mean.

*Where the software analogy fits:* reliability engineering. You care about p99 latency, not mean latency. An intervention with a good mean and a fat left tail is a service that is fast on average and times out for 5% of users, and in schools that 5% is disproportionately the students already most disadvantaged. *Where it breaks:* teacher variation is not configuration drift you fix by reverting to a known-good build. It comes from skill, context, relationships and student mix; you reduce it by building capability and support, not by enforcing a spec. And the goal is less variation in **outcomes**, not uniform practice; positive deviants are to be learned from, not flattened.

**Principle: see the system that produces the current outcomes.** A saying from healthcare improvement, usually credited to Paul Batalden: every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets. Before changing anything, map how the result is produced.
- **Process map**: the actual steps (how a failing grade becomes an intervention, or does not). Leaks cluster at handoffs and unowned steps. Fresno Unified mapped the path from high school to college as a leaky pipeline and found many losses were **procedural** (forms, deadlines, missing information, course placement), not a lack of ability or ambition. That is funnel analytics, broken out by subgroup, and the analogy holds well.
- **Fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram**, built with the people who do the work, then checked against data. Steer toward causes inside the school's control without pretending outside causes do not matter.
- **Pareto chart**: rank causes by frequency. Often most course failures come from missing assignments rather than failed tests, which tells you where to act first.

*Analogy:* the **blameless post-incident review**. Not *who broke production?* but *what about our system made this failure likely, and why did no safeguard catch it?* A student failing a course is an incident; look for contributing factors. *Where it breaks:* software leaves logs. In schools, causes are spread out, often invisible (a home situation, a friendship ending) and slow to appear, so every root-cause analysis is a **hypothesis**, not a finding.

**The folk theory to retire** is the one behind most staffroom conversations: bad outcomes come from bad people. Mostly they come from processes nobody designed.

ideas.title: Aim and driver diagram: your theory of improvement, written down and revisable
ideas.body:
Bryk's first principle: **make the work problem-specific and user-centered.** Start from a precisely stated problem, not a solution. *38% of our ninth graders fail at least one core course in fall semester* is a problem. *Let's adopt a tutoring platform* is a solution looking for one; Carnegie calls the habit **solutionitis**, and it is the default failure of leadership teams. Understand the problem as the people who live it do: interview students and teachers, shadow a student's day, map their journey.

*Analogy (a good fit):* product discovery, jobs-to-be-done, falling in love with the problem. *Where it breaks:* your users are required to attend, teachers are both users of the system and the people delivering it, and what a 14-year-old wants (less homework) is not always their long-term interest. User-centered here means serving their long-run interests with judgment, which a satisfaction survey cannot supply.

**The aim statement**: how much, by when, for whom. Example: by June of year two, 90% of ninth graders pass all core courses, with no gap across income or racial subgroups. It works like an OKR except it names the population and the distribution, not only the average.

**The driver diagram** is the single most important tool to learn. Read left to right:
- **Aim**: the measurable outcome.
- **Primary drivers**: the few (typically 3-5) areas you believe must change. For ninth-grade course passing: students' academic mindsets, quality of core instruction, an early-warning and response system, transition supports.
- **Secondary drivers**: the specific structures, processes and norms acting on each primary driver. Under early warning: timely grade data visible to teachers; a weekly team meeting on at-risk students; a clear menu of responses.
- **Change ideas**: specific, testable changes. Example: advisors text families the same day a student misses a major assignment.

Two properties make it more than a slide. First, it is a **hypothesis meant to be revised**: PDSA cycles show which drivers actually move the aim, and you update the diagram, like a living architecture decision record. Second, **every node carries a measure**: outcome measures at the aim, driver measures in the middle, process measures at the change ideas. The diagram *is* your measurement plan. Software analogy: a metrics tree bound to a causal hypothesis.

**How it disciplines a school.** Maintain one driver diagram per annual aim, owned by a small improvement team and reviewed each term. Every proposed initiative must attach to a driver or be declined, which is Wiliam's not-doing list (Module 8) given a mechanism. Keep aims to two or three a year [E for focus as an improvement principle; H for the number].

**Where the other books plug in.** A driver diagram is only as good as the theory in it. Module 1-6 content supplies high-quality drivers: retrieval and spacing, formative assessment, knowledge-rich curriculum, belonging and mentor-mindset feedback. Yeager's belonging and productive-persistence work literally supplied drivers for the Carnegie Math Pathways, the community-college network that redesigned remedial maths into credit-bearing statistics and quantitative reasoning courses (Statway and Quantway). Transcend's Graduate Aims and Leaps (Module 7) belong at the *aim* level (what the community wants), not in the drivers, which should be constrained by evidence.

**Tag it [H].** The driver diagram is a disciplined way to hold a theory; the theory in any particular diagram is a hypothesis until your cycles and measures say otherwise.

ideas.title: Measure for improvement: practical measures, and the four kinds you need
ideas.body:
Bryk's fourth principle: **we cannot improve at scale what we cannot measure.** Schools are usually drowning in measurement and starved of the right kind.

**Three purposes, three kinds of measure**
- **Accountability measures** (annual state tests, inspection grades) exist to judge. They are lagging, coarse, and arrive long after the year you could have acted. Using them to drive weekly improvement produces gaming and despair.
- **Research measures** (long validated scales) exist to publish. They are rigorous, slow and burdensome; using them for improvement produces paralysis.
- **Practical measures** exist to guide the next change. Most schools have plenty of the first two and none of the third.

**Practical measures** (Yeager, Bryk, Muhich, Hausman & Morales 2013, *Practical Measurement*; note Yeager is the author of Module 3's book) are:
- **specific to the change** being tested, not a general construct;
- **fast and cheap**: a few items, seconds to minutes, repeated often;
- **predictive**: shown to relate to the outcome you care about;
- **actionable**: back in the practitioner's hands this week, in a usable form;
- **low stakes**: never used to evaluate people, or they get gamed.
The Carnegie Math Pathways used a handful of short productive-persistence survey items, answered in seconds at key moments, to flag students at risk early. In your school: weekly count of drafts submitted per student, pulled from the platform you already use; the share of students choosing a misconception distractor on this unit's hinge question; minutes from bell to first student task.

*Analogy (a strong fit):* **observability**. The annual test is quarterly revenue, a lagging indicator. You need the equivalent of request-level metrics and traces: leading indicators close enough to the work to show whether this week's change did anything. *Where it breaks, three ways:* (1) measuring people changes their behavior (Campbell's law, Goodhart's law); servers do not game dashboards, teachers and students do. (2) Every measure costs instructional time and goodwill. (3) Much of what you care about (understanding, belonging, curiosity) can only be measured noisily. This is Mehta & Fine's warning: a narrow measurement culture can quietly push out depth.

**Four kinds of measure for every change** (from the healthcare improvement tradition):
- **Outcome**: did the aim move? Lagging.
- **Driver**: did the hypothesized lever move (sense of belonging, share of teachers using early-warning data)?
- **Process**: was the change actually done as planned (share of families contacted within 24 hours)? Without it you cannot tell a bad idea from a badly executed one.
- **Balancing**: did we break something else (teacher workload, time lost from core classes, student stress)? These are guardrail metrics, and they are the ones most often forgotten.

**Separating the systems.** Keep improvement data physically and culturally separate from evaluation. Never feed practical measures into teacher appraisal [E that high-stakes use corrupts indicators; V for choosing trust over surveillance]. Accountability measures are reported, not managed to. A diagnostic across two years: if practical measures improve and accountability measures do not, your drivers are probably wrong; if the reverse, suspect gaming or teaching to the test.

**Read charts properly.** Plot measures over time with changes marked. Deming's distinction between **common-cause** variation (the system's normal noise) and **special-cause** variation (a real signal) stops you reacting to every weekly wobble. Simple run-chart rules (for example, six or more consecutive points above the median) help, but with small, noisy classroom samples false signals are easy to see. Treat a single good week as a rumor.

ideas.title: PDSA: small, predicted tests, and why they are not A/B tests
ideas.body:
Bryk's fifth principle: anchor practice improvement in **disciplined inquiry**. The unit is the **Plan-Do-Study-Act** cycle, organized by the Model for Improvement (Langley and colleagues, *The Improvement Guide*) and its three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know a change is an improvement? What change can we make that will result in improvement?

**The cycle**
- **Plan**: state the change, **a written prediction**, and how you will measure it. Who, where, when.
- **Do**: run it small: one teacher, one class, one or two weeks.
- **Study**: compare what happened with what you predicted. The gap is the learning.
- **Act**: adopt, adapt or abandon, and plan the next cycle.
Then build **ramps**: a series of cycles growing in scale and in the variety of conditions (one teacher, three, a department, the school). Scale only when the change holds across contexts. Bryk's slogan: **learning fast to implement well**. Fail small and fast so you do not fail large and slow.

**Why the prediction is the whole point.** Without one, no result can surprise you, so your theory of the system is never tested or revised; you simply narrate whatever happened as success. The prediction is also the main protection against fooling yourself. Healthcare reviews of PDSA use find it is often done without rigor: no prediction, poor documentation, cycles that do not build on each other. In many districts *continuous improvement* has decayed into templates filled in after the fact, a lethal mutation of the method itself.

*Analogy (partial):* feature flags and canary releases. Ship to 1%, watch the metrics, widen the rollout; the ramp logic transfers well. *Where it breaks, and this matters:* **a PDSA cycle is not an A/B test.** An A/B test uses randomization and large samples to estimate a causal effect with known confidence. A PDSA cycle is usually n = 1 classroom with no control group. It builds practical knowledge by accumulating many small, predicted, observed tests, read on run charts with judgment, and replicated across contexts. It is closer to a developer iterating on a local build against a clear spec. Its failure modes are regression to the mean, novelty effects, and a good week that had nothing to do with the change. And **students cannot be rolled back**: a failed test used real children's learning time, which is why tests start so small and why settled science should constrain what you test.

**What PDSA is for, and not for.** Use it to make proven practices work reliably *here*: how to run hinge questions in Year 7 maths with 30 students and a 50-minute period, how to get redraft time to actually happen, how to make the early-warning meeting produce action. Do not use it to rediscover pedagogy from scratch. Local PDSA results are not evidence on a par with decades of cognitive science; the science should decide which change ideas are worth testing.

**The same loop at three scales.** Formative assessment (Module 6) is PDSA inside a lesson: elicit evidence, interpret, adjust. A TLC is PDSA for a teacher's practice: commit to a technique, try it, report back, revise. Improvement science is formative assessment applied to the institution. Transcend's Test-Drive (Module 7) is a PDSA ramp for a newly designed experience; run it with Bryk's discipline of prediction, practical measures and balancing measures.

**Tag it [H].** The method has a strong record in manufacturing and a substantial but mixed one in healthcare; in schools the evidence is mostly case-based. Its value depends entirely on keeping the discipline.

ideas.title: Networks, hubs, leadership, and what the cases can and cannot prove
ideas.body:
Bryk's sixth principle: **accelerate learning through networked improvement communities (NICs).** A single school learns slowly: few cases, little variation, no way to tell local luck from a real effect. A network of schools working on the *same* problem, with a shared aim, a shared driver diagram, shared measures and a coordinating hub, runs tests in many contexts at once and sees what holds up. *Analogy (reasonable):* an open-source project with a common roadmap, shared test suite and maintainers who merge contributions. *Where it breaks:* NICs depend on trust and voluntary participation across organizations with different bosses, calendars and incentives, and hubs need long-term funding. None of it is as cheap as a pull request.

**The six cases** (read them as organizational capability, not programs):
- **Fresno Unified**: mapped the leaky pipeline to college; many losses were procedural and fixable.
- **New Visions for Public Schools** (NYC): an **analytic hub** building tools that give counselors and teachers a live, student-by-student view of credits, exam requirements and attendance, treating practitioners as users. Data helps only inside routines that say who looks, when, and what they do next. Staff this role at your school like an internal-tools product owner; the classic failure is dashboards nobody opens.
- **Summit Public Schools**: a radical redesign treated as continuous learning, not a launch. You are Summit: v1 will fail in ways you cannot predict, so budget roles, time and data for learning from the first term. (Its personalized-learning platform later drew controversy in some adopting districts; the book does not settle whether the model works elsewhere.)
- **High Tech High**: even a strong, admired pedagogy hid inequitable outcomes until data were broken out by subgroup. Improvement had to be framed as professional inquiry, not compliance.
- **National Writing Project, College-Ready Writers Program**: a NIC on a classroom problem (argument writing). An independent SRI randomized trial found positive effects on teacher practice and student writing, one of the rare places improvement work has RCT support, though for the whole package of content, professional learning and routines.
- **Menomonee Falls** (Wisconsin): under superintendent Pat Greco, everyone was trained in improvement methods, from teachers and operations staff to the board and students; culture moved from blame to learning. The DevOps-transformation analogy fits, including the lesson that it is mostly culture. Risk: dependence on one leader.

**Leadership decides whether any of this works.** Leaders set aims, give time and roles, make it safe to surface failure, and model inquiry. Improvement run as compliance becomes paperwork. Transcend's learner-centered leadership and routine maintenance point the same way.

**What the book can and cannot prove.** These are case narratives, chosen because they went well, about Carnegie partners, largely from leaders' own accounts, with no comparison groups. They show that improvement practices can be adopted and are associated with improving trends; they cannot show the methods caused those trends, or how often such efforts fail. The cases also concentrate on **measurable secondary-school outcomes** (graduation, credits, attendance, college access). Do not assume transfer is equally easy to hard-to-measure goals like understanding or curiosity. Improvement routines consume adult time, so count that as a balancing measure.

**Institutional design for a founder** [mostly H]: two or three annual aims with subgroup breakdowns; a student-level funnel and early-warning system from day one (early-warning indicators such as attendance and course failure predict later outcomes well [E, Chicago on-track research]); an improvement lead; protected weekly inquiry time; blameless reviews of student failures; all staff trained in basic methods; join or found a NIC; and succession planning, so the system lives in roles and routines, not one person.

worked_example.title: Decision: the school's improvement operating system
steps: Choose one primary aim for year one, stated for a population and a distribution: for example, by June, 85% of Year 7 students reach the unit mastery threshold in maths on the delayed end-of-unit check, with no gap by prior attainment or income. [E for the method of precise aims; V for choosing this aim]

Before choosing solutions, see the system: break current results out by class, teacher and subgroup; Pareto the reasons (missing practice? misconceptions surviving the unit? absences?); shadow two students for a day; map what happens when a student falls behind. Look for positive deviants among your own teachers. [E for the diagnostic stance; H for what you will find]

Draw the driver diagram with an improvement team of three to five people: for example, primary drivers of retrieval and spaced practice built into lessons, in-lesson formative checks acted on, time on task in the first ten minutes, and belonging in maths. Every initiative must attach to a driver or be declined. [H]

Attach a measure to each level: outcome (delayed unit check), driver (hinge-question distractor rates; a two-item belonging pulse each fortnight), process (share of lessons with a planned all-student check), balancing (teacher planning hours; student stress item). [E for the four-measure structure; H for the specific measures]

Run PDSA cycles of two to four weeks, each with a written prediction before it starts and a 30-minute study meeting at the end: roughly three cycles per team per term, ramping from one class to the department only when a change holds. [E for disciplined small tests as method; H for the cadence]

Keep practical measures in a lightweight dashboard separate from the gradebook, and never use them in appraisal. Report accountability measures; do not manage to them. [V; E that high-stakes use corrupts indicators]
Wire the TLCs from Module 6 in as the classroom-level instance of the same loop, and use community codesign sessions from Module 7 to shape the aim, not the drivers. [H; V]
Hold a blameless review whenever a student fails a course: contributing factors, not culprits, feeding the fishbone. [H]
Look outward: find two or three peer schools working on the same problem and share the driver diagram and measures; a network sees variation a single school cannot. [H]
Policy line for the brief: Every change is a test with a prediction; improvement data is for learning, never for judging.

hinge.q: Bryk's principle 'see the system that produces the current outcomes' means:
options: Hold everyone accountable for the outcome, because a system in which each person owns a result is one that produces it
Adopt a coherent whole-school program, because a fragmented set of initiatives is the system failure most schools suffer
Build data dashboards so leaders can see results, because outcomes made visible in real time let the system correct itself
Map the actual processes, handoffs and conditions that produce the outcome, including the ones nobody designed or notices
diagnoses: Accountability equals system. Assigning blame to people is exactly what 'every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets' warns against.
Program equals system. Programs are solutions; seeing the system is diagnosis, and it comes first.
Tools equal seeing. Dashboards show outcomes, not the process producing them; New Visions' lesson is that data helps only inside routines.
Correct. Process maps, fishbones and conversations with the people doing the work reveal where results are actually produced, like a blameless incident review.

hinge.q: A PDSA cycle run without a written prediction is deficient mainly because:
options: Predictions are required for research ethics, so a cycle without one cannot be shared or written up as improvement science
Without a prediction the result cannot surprise you, so the theory of the system is never tested and never has to be revised
Nobody will remember what was planned, so at the study step the team cannot tell what it changed from what it merely intended
Predictions motivate the team, so a cycle without one loses the commitment that carries a change through its first hard weeks
diagnoses: Compliance reading. PDSA is not a research protocol; this confuses improvement with research measurement.
Correct. The gap between prediction and result is the learning, and writing it down first is the main defense against narrating any outcome as success.
Documentation reading. Record-keeping matters, but you could document a plan perfectly and still learn nothing.
Motivational reading. Any motivational effect is incidental; the function is epistemic.

hinge.q: Which of these is a practical measure, in Bryk's sense, for the change 'students revise their writing'?
options: A weekly count of drafts submitted per student, pulled from the platform already in use, because it is cheap, frequent and specific
A validated 40-item writing self-efficacy scale given each term, because a measure with known reliability is worth the extra time
The end-of-year state writing score, because it is the outcome the school is judged on and the one measure everyone trusts
The teacher's overall impression at the end of the unit, because the person closest to the work sees what no instrument captures
diagnoses: Correct. It is specific to the change, cheap, frequent, embedded in the work and back in teachers' hands within days, and it stays low stakes.
Research measure. Rigorous but slow, burdensome and not specific to the change; it produces paralysis, not iteration.
Accountability measure used for improvement. It is lagging and coarse, and arrives too late to guide any change this term.
Too vague to detect change. An impression is not comparable week to week and is open to confirmation bias.

hinge.q: A teammate says: 'A PDSA cycle is basically an A/B test for teachers.' What is the best correction?
options: Right, and that is why each cycle needs a control group, because without one you cannot tell the change from everything else going on in the school
Right, except that PDSA uses larger samples, because a whole school runs the change rather than the two arms of an A/B test
Wrong: a PDSA is usually n = 1 with no control; it builds practical knowledge through many small predicted tests, run charts and replication
Wrong: PDSA cycles are qualitative and use no data, because improvement is a matter of professional judgement rather than measurement
diagnoses: Imports the A/B frame. Adding a control to every two-week classroom test is usually impractical and misses how PDSA builds knowledge.
Reverses the facts. PDSA samples are smaller, which is exactly why self-deception is the main risk.
Correct. The ramp logic resembles a canary release, but the inference is different; its protections are the prior prediction, run charts and replication, and students cannot be rolled back.
Overcorrection. PDSA relies on practical measures and run charts; it is disciplined and quantitative where possible.

hinge.q: Your new advisory program raises attendance. Which is a balancing measure you should also be tracking?
options: Attendance rate, because the measure the program set out to move is the one that must be watched for slippage after the launch
Students' sense of belonging, because the mechanism through which advisory is supposed to raise attendance must also be checked
The share of advisors who ran the session as planned, because a gain in attendance means little if the program was not delivered
Advisor workload and instructional time lost from core classes, because a gain in one place can quietly break something elsewhere
diagnoses: That is the outcome measure: it tells you whether the aim moved, not what else changed.
That is a driver measure if belonging is a hypothesized lever for attendance.
That is a process measure: it tells you whether the change was carried out as designed.
Correct. Balancing measures are guardrail metrics that catch improvement in one place quietly breaking something else, and teacher workload is the most often forgotten.

State how improvement data is kept separate from appraisal. Then open your brief's Open Hypotheses register and convert three [H] items from earlier modules into PDSA cycles with predictions.
