modules.title: Integration: tensions, decision rules, and the unified model
modules.hook: You have now met a dozen authors who seem to disagree about almost everything: explicit teaching versus struggle first, knowledge versus curiosity, standard mechanisms versus community design, measurement versus depth. What if most of those fights disappear once you ask four questions: for whom, for what goal, at what point in expertise, and with what consolidation?

attempt.prompt: Before reading on, and without looking back at earlier modules: write down the five biggest disagreements among the authors you have met. For each, write (a) who you side with, (b) under what specific conditions you would switch sides, and (c) what you would observe in your own school that would tell you it is time to switch. Then take your Brief v0 from Module 0 and, in the margin, re-tag three claims as E, H or V. You will compare both against the model and rules below.

objectives: Reproduce the unified three-band model (minds, design, institution) and the improvement loop from memory, and explain each arrow.
For each major tension, state the conditional decision rule, the evidence behind each branch, and the switch signal.
Trace any institutional policy down to the mind-level mechanism it relies on and back up through a practical measure.
Explain why institutions improve through the same mechanisms that make children learn (the symmetry principle), and design for it.
Re-tag Brief v0 correctly, explaining each original tagging error and which module corrected it.

ideas.title: The unified model: three bands, constraints up, enablement down, and a loop
ideas.body:
Everything in this course fits one picture. Draw it from memory until you can.

**Band 1, Minds (bottom; mostly [E]).**
- **Working memory**: tiny and fragile, the bottleneck for new material (Sweller).
- **Long-term memory**: schemas, the seat of expertise; strengthened by effortful retrieval, spacing, and errors followed by correction (Roediger & Karpicke, Cepeda, Bjork, Ranganath).
- **Prior knowledge**: coherent intuitive theories that assimilate new input and are suppressed, never deleted (Shtulman, Posner, Chi, Vosniadou, Amin).
- **Motivational state**: curiosity as an information gap that needs knowledge to exist (Gruber, Gelman & Ranganath 2014; Engel), and adolescent sensitivity to status and respect (Yeager).

**Band 2, Design (middle; [E] for mechanisms, [H] for parameters).**
- **Instruction**: explicit by default, generate-then-consolidate when its conditions hold, guidance fading with expertise (Kirschner, Rosenshine, Kapur).
- **Curriculum**: coherent, cumulative, knowledge-rich; concepts sequenced by prerequisite (Wexler, Wiliam, Shtulman).
- **Assessment**: formative, hinge questions, comment-only feedback, success criteria (Wiliam & Leahy).
- **Relationship**: mentor mindset, wise feedback, question-welcoming norms (Yeager, Engel).

**Band 3, Institution (top; [H] and [V] heavy).**
- **Adult learning**: TLCs, hiring for learnability, development over selection (Wiliam).
- **Structure**: schedule, grouping, the grammar of school, apprenticeship features in the core (Mehta & Fine).
- **Community and purpose**: codesign, which knowledge counts, identity (Samouha et al., Mehta & Fine).
- **Improvement system**: aim, driver diagram, PDSA, practical measures (Bryk).

**Upward arrows mean *constrains*.** Load limits pacing and guidance. Schemas determine readiness. Intuitive theories determine what must be confronted. Status determines how feedback lands. No institutional or design choice can repeal a band below it; a schedule that ignores spacing, or a feedback policy that ignores status, fails no matter how good it looks on the org chart.

**Downward arrows mean *enables*.** Adult learning makes the right instructional default easy. Structure gives it time and audience. Community decides what is worth knowing. The institution does not teach anyone directly; it makes good design the path of least resistance for every adult, every day.

**The loop is the point.** From the improvement system, practical measures reach down to what is happening in minds (retrieval accuracy, misconception rates on hinge questions, redraft rates, question rates, belonging pulses), and predictions tested there revise the defaults above. **The institution is the thing that learns.**

**Read the badges.** Certainty declines as you go up. Band 1 rests on laboratory and classroom experiments replicated for decades. Band 2 mechanisms are well supported, but parameters (how long, how often, which technique) are local bets. Band 3 rests on a few trials at scale (the EEF formative assessment trial, Tennessee STAR, the Writing Project's RCT), observational case studies (Mehta & Fine, Bryk, Transcend), and values. If your brief's institutional section is mostly [E], you are over-claiming.

**How to use the model.** For any proposal, trace a path. Down: which design mechanism does it enable, and which mind-level constraint does that mechanism respect? Back up: what practical measure would show it working in minds, and which default would you revise if it did not? A proposal with no traceable path (a device rollout justified as engagement, a new schedule justified as innovation) is decoration. A proposal whose path breaks a lower-band constraint is a mistake, however popular. [H: the model is this course's synthesis, not a finding of any single book.]

ideas.title: Design-level tensions are resolved by conditions, not winners
ideas.body:
The instructional debates in this curriculum mostly dissolve once you specify for whom, for what goal, at what point in expertise, and with what consolidation. Each rule below has an evidence base on both branches and a **switch signal**: what you would observe in your own school that says change course.

**1. Explicit instruction vs. productive failure** (Kirschner, Sweller & Clark vs. Kapur). **Rule:** default to explicit instruction with worked examples, fading guidance as expertise grows (the expertise-reversal effect). Use generate-then-consolidate only when all four hold: the goal is conceptual understanding or transfer, not procedure; learners have relevant prior knowledge to activate; the problem admits several plausible approaches; and a scripted consolidation compares student methods with the canonical one. Evidence: Kapur's meta-analysis finds benefits for conceptual knowledge and transfer (about g = 0.36, higher with faithful design) and none for procedural knowledge (about -0.03), with larger effects from grade 6 upward. PF is not discovery learning; it satisfies Kirschner's core mechanism because full instruction follows. Never use unguided discovery with novices. **Switch:** if observations show rushed, muddled consolidation, or procedural fluency drops on practical measures, revert to explicit teaching for that unit.

**2. Knowledge vs. curiosity** (Wexler and Wiliam vs. Engel). Largely a false tension. Gruber, Gelman & Ranganath showed curiosity enhances memory for its target, and curiosity requires enough knowledge to notice a gap. Engel's evidence is real, though: children ask far more questions at home than at school (Tizard & Hughes 1984), and demonstration narrows exploration (Bonawitz et al. 2011). **Rule:** a knowledge-rich curriculum is the substrate; curiosity is protected by classroom norms (questions answered and followed up, uncertainty modeled, pacing that allows detours, open the question before giving the answer), not by content-free exploration time. Put the learning objective inside the question, since curiosity's spillover to unrelated material is small and can reverse. **Switch:** if question rates per hour fall year on year, fix the norms, not the curriculum.

**3. Confront misconceptions vs. avoid showing them.** Posner's conditions require dissatisfaction plus an intelligible, plausible, fruitful alternative; Shtulman & Valcarcel (2012) show intuitive theories are suppressed rather than deleted. **Rule:** confront, but only once the correct model is intelligible, with immediate correction, and never leave the wrong model as the last thing students see. Teach mechanism, not just conclusions. **Switch:** if hinge-question distractor rates for a misconception *rise* after a confrontation lesson, students are remembering the confrontation as the content; restructure.

**4. Testing as measurement vs. testing as learning.** Retrieval changes memory (Roediger & Karpicke; Ranganath), and errors followed promptly by correction are learning events. **Rule:** most testing exists for learning: frequent, low stakes, cumulative, comment-only, spaced. A small number of summative points exist for reporting. **Switch:** if students or families treat every check as a judgment, the framing has failed; rename and reframe before changing the practice.

**5. How feedback lands.** High standards and high support are a combination, not a midpoint (Yeager). **Rule:** critique paired with an explicit statement of the high bar and belief the student can meet it; task-focused, never ego-focused (Kluger & DeNisi). **Switch:** if compliance rises while effort quality falls, you have drifted to enforcer; if satisfaction rises while effort quality falls, to protector.

Notice the shape of every rule: a **default**, **named conditions for the exception**, and an **observable trigger** for switching. That is a decision rule a new teacher can use on a Tuesday, which is what makes it institutional rather than philosophical.

ideas.title: Institution-level tensions: six rules with switch signals
ideas.body:
The institutional tensions have thinner evidence, so the rules are hypotheses to run, not settled answers. Hold each with its switch signal.

**1. Standardization vs. community design** (Wiliam and Wexler's coherence vs. Samouha et al.'s codesign). **Rule:** standardize the mechanisms (retrieval, feedback, TLCs, the default lesson) and the knowledge sequence within each discipline; codesign purpose, culture, the periphery, and knowledge priorities where evidence is silent [V]. Write down in the founding compact which layer is open. **Switch:** if codesign sessions start proposing to change mechanisms (drop phonics, match learning styles), that is a governance failure. Honor the underlying need and answer it in the open layer.

**2. Accountability vs. improvement** (external regimes vs. Bryk). **Rule:** keep the two measurement systems physically and culturally separate. Improvement measures never enter evaluation; accountability measures are reported, not managed to. **Switch:** if practical measures improve for two years while accountability measures do not, your drivers are wrong; if the reverse, someone is gaming or teaching to the test.

**3. Mastery vs. identity and creativity** (No Excuses High vs. Dewey High). **Rule:** mastery first in the core, built on a knowledge sequence and explicit teaching, with one authentic product per course per term; identity and creativity also concentrated in a protected periphery every student joins, with mixed-age leadership ladders. **Switch:** if the periphery becomes the only place students say they learn, the core has failed. If core scores rise and student voice collapses, the periphery is being starved, or the core has drifted to enforcer.

**4. Selecting vs. developing teachers** (folk hire-the-best vs. Wiliam). **Rule:** develop. Hire for disciplinary depth and coachability using work samples; make years one to three a structured development program; TLCs for everyone, indefinitely. **Switch:** if after three years of TLCs the within-school spread in teacher effectiveness has not narrowed, the TLC design is broken. The usual causes are no real accountability for trying techniques, TLC time cannibalized, or turnover.

**5. Structural vs. instructional reform** (schedule and model enthusiasts, and Mehta & Fine's restructuring agenda, vs. Wiliam's cost evidence). **Rule:** spend change capacity on instruction, assessment, curriculum and adult learning first. Keep structure conventional unless a specific instructional need requires a change (for example, longer blocks for lab or studio work), and run that change as a named hypothesis. Remember that a new, independent school gains nothing from its container alone. **Switch:** if instructional work is blocked by structure (no common time for TLCs; no slot for redrafting), change structure minimally and deliberately.

**6. Adolescent autonomy vs. adult direction** (enforcer and protector vs. Yeager's mentor). **Rule:** high standards with high support, transparency about why, sincere questions, and choice within structure. Discipline systems and advisory are audited against this, not only lessons. **Switch:** compliance up while effort quality falls means enforcer drift; satisfaction up while effort quality falls means protector drift.

**Three patterns across all six.**
- The resolution is almost always **layering**: fix one layer by evidence, open another to values or local choice, and write down which is which. Wiliam's *tight but loose* is the same move applied to teacher practice.
- Every rule needs an **observable switch signal**, which means a practical measure (Module 9) must exist before the tension becomes live. If you cannot name the signal, you cannot run the rule.
- The failure modes are **drift**, not dramatic reversal: enforcer drift, periphery starvation, measures quietly entering appraisal, codesign quietly touching mechanisms. Drift is detected by routine maintenance (Transcend) and run charts (Bryk), not by annual strategy retreats.

ideas.title: Symmetry: the institution learns through the same mechanisms as the child
ideas.body:
The deepest integration in this curriculum is that the Band 1 mechanisms apply to adults and to the organization itself. Several authors state versions of this independently. Mehta & Fine's **symmetry principle**: teachers need the conditions the school wants for students. Kirschner & Hendrick's closing warning: the central problem for a school is not choosing practices but preserving their active ingredient at scale. Bryk: improvement is an organizational capability. Put together, they give you a design method: **design adult and organizational learning with the same science you use for children.**

**Working memory → initiative overload.** A staff juggling eight initiatives is a working memory with too many interacting elements; nothing gets encoded into routine. Wiliam's two or three priorities and a not-doing list is cognitive load theory applied to a faculty.

**Novices need worked examples → new staff need worked examples too.** Expertise reversal applies to teachers. A first-year teacher asked to run an open-ended inquiry cycle on their own practice is a novice given minimal guidance. Give them scripted routines, model lessons, and worked examples of good improvement work first, then fade. Improvement inquiry, like student inquiry, works best for people with enough knowledge to use it.

**Spacing and retrieval → the TLC cadence.** Monthly meetings over two years are spaced practice for adults: try the technique, return a month later to retrieve and report on it, revise. A two-day workshop is massed practice, which Module 1 predicts will feel productive and fade.

**Feedback that can hurt → appraisal design.** Kluger & DeNisi's finding applies to teachers: feedback aimed at the self (ratings, rankings, *needs improvement*) tends to lower performance; task-focused, forward-looking feedback helps. Hence non-evaluative peer observation focused on the teacher's own chosen technique, and a hard wall between improvement data and appraisal.

**Status and respect → the mentor mindset for adults.** Teachers, like adolescents, resist being treated as incompetent or controlled. Mandating a technique and inspecting for it (the traffic-light principal of Module 6) is the enforcer mindset; letting everyone do as they please is the protector. TLCs (choice plus accountability) and learner-centered leadership are the mentor version.

**Formative assessment at three scales.** Elicit evidence, interpret, adjust. In a lesson it is the hinge question. For a teacher it is the TLC's report-back-and-commit cycle. For the institution it is the PDSA cycle with a prediction, a practical measure and a balancing measure. It is one loop at three zoom levels. If your school does it well at one level and not the others, expect the others to erode it.

**Misconceptions → lethal mutations.** Children's intuitive theories assimilate new instruction into old models, producing synthetic models. Organizations do the same to new practices: the grammar of school absorbs reforms (Tyack & Cuban), and techniques keep their names while losing their active ingredients. The countermeasures rhyme too: name the active ingredient explicitly (like teaching the mechanism), watch for the characteristic mutation (like a diagnostic distractor), and **codify** routines in writing so they survive turnover (Van Ness).

**Curiosity and identity → retention.** Mehta & Fine's deepest teachers had learned deeply in a field; teachers whose own practice is a field of inquiry stay and grow (Kraft & Papay: growth continues longer in supportive environments).

**Design test for your brief.** For each adult-facing structure (hiring, onboarding, TLCs, observation, meetings, appraisal), ask: would I design a child's learning this way? If you would never teach a novice with a single lecture, massed and followed by a graded verdict, do not onboard teachers that way either. [H: the symmetry is a strong, cross-book synthesis; its specific applications are hypotheses to test.]

ideas.title: Tagging discipline: evidence, hypothesis, value, and re-tagging your v0
ideas.body:
The E/H/V tags are not bureaucracy. They are how a founder avoids the most common failure in education: **laundering values and hunches as evidence**, then being unable to learn because nothing was ever framed as testable.

**What each tag means**
- **[E] Evidence**: a mechanism or effect with convergent, replicated support, ideally including causal designs. Even within [E], strength varies: a large randomized trial at scale (EEF formative assessment, Tennessee STAR, the Writing Project RCT) beats a meta-analysis of small studies, which beats a single lab finding, which beats an observational case study. Name the strength when it matters.
- **[H] Hypothesis**: plausible, mechanism-grounded, but untested in your form or context. An [H] is a promise to test: it belongs in your Open Hypotheses register with the PDSA cycle or evidence that would resolve it.
- **[V] Value**: a commitment about what matters that evidence cannot settle (which knowledge counts, equity of access, joy, community voice). A [V] is not weaker than an [E]; it is a different kind of claim. Register it with one sentence on who might reasonably disagree.

**Split mixed sentences.** Most real design claims mix types. *Every teacher joins a monthly 90-minute TLC for two years, separate from appraisal* is [E] for the package (a trial at scale), [H] for the parameters (size, cadence are defaults), and [V] for the separation (a trust commitment with plausible but untested psychology). Tag each part.

**The typical v0 errors, and which module fixes them**
- *Students learn best by discovering things for themselves* tagged [E]: contradicted by the novice-guidance evidence. Rewrite with conditions (Modules 1, 4).
- *Teaching to learning styles* in any form: delete (Module 1).
- *Small classes will drive our results* tagged [E] with no caveat: [E] that effects are real, modest and expensive; the strategic claim fails on cost (Module 8).
- *We will be excellent because we are independent and innovative*: contradicted by choice-sector evidence; autonomy is an option, not an asset (Module 8).
- *Project-based learning produces deeper learning* tagged [E]: [H]. Mehta & Fine's periphery pattern is observational and selection-confounded, and Dewey High shows the failure mode (Module 7).
- *We'll use data to track progress*: untaggable until it names the decision the data changes and the cycle length (Modules 6, 9).
- *Every child deserves to be known by an adult* tagged [E]: it is [V] (with some [E] behind belonging). Tagging it [V] makes it stronger, not weaker, because nobody can refute it with a study.
- *Hire the best teachers* as the strategy: [E] contradicts it as a primary lever; replace it with develop-over-select (Module 8).
- *Formative assessment will add half a year of learning*: effect-size naivety; plan for about 0.1 SD at scale (Modules 6, 8).

**Heuristics for honest tagging**
- Obviousness is not evidence: an unstudied obvious claim is [V] or [H].
- If a claim cites one admired school, it is [H] at best.
- If a claim quotes an effect size, it must also say age, test type and cost, or it is not yet [E] for your decision.
- If your Band 3 sections are mostly [E], you are over-claiming; if they are mostly [V], you are hiding from scrutiny.
- Every [H] should name its switch signal and its first test.

**The point for a founder.** A brief tagged this way is an operating document. The [E] claims become defaults you defend. The [H] claims become your first year of PDSA cycles. The [V] claims become the charter you recruit families and staff around.

worked_example.title: One path through the whole model: comment-only marking, traced down to minds and back up through the loop
steps: Institution band, the policy: formative work receives comments only; every comment requires a student response in protected lesson time; grades appear at a few summative points per term. [E for the mechanism; H for the cadence]

Institution band, adult learning: the policy is built as a habit through TLCs, where teachers choose a feedback technique (find it and fix it, whole-class feedback) and report back monthly. Tight on the active ingredient (students act on comments), loose on the technique. Anticipated lethal mutation: comments written, no response time given. [E for the TLC package; H for the specifics]

Design band, assessment: feedback that moves learning forward. Butler: grades cancel comments. Kluger & DeNisi: self-focused feedback often lowers performance, task-focused feedback helps. Ramaprasad: feedback exists only if used to close the gap. Exemplars and success criteria make the gap visible. [E]

Design band, relationship: how the comment lands depends on trust and status. A wise-feedback frame (high standard, stated belief the student can meet it) raised revision dramatically in Yeager's study, most among students with least reason to trust school. [E]

Minds band, why it works: without a grade, attention stays on the task rather than on ranking (task- vs. ego-involvement; Boekaerts' growth vs. well-being pathways). The required response is generation and retrieval, which strengthen memory. Correcting a flagged error is a prediction-error learning event (Ranganath). A comment focused on one or two criteria respects working-memory limits, and a comment that names the specific misconception targets the prior-knowledge structure that needs to change. [E]

Back up the loop, practical measures: weekly redraft rate per class (process), quality gain between draft and redraft on a small rubric sample (driver), share of students making the same error on the next task (driver). Balancing measures: teacher marking hours, and family complaints about missing grades. [H for these specific measures]
Prediction, written before term one: redraft rate above 80% by week six; marking hours flat or down; the repeat-error rate on the targeted misconception halves by the end of the unit. [H]

Switch signals: if redraft rates rise but quality gains do not, comments are too vague, so fix comment quality in TLCs. If families read every check as a judgment, the framing has failed, so rename and reframe before changing the practice. If marking hours rise, the policy has mutated into more writing, so cut volume. [H]
The lesson: every institutional policy should have a traceable path down to a mind-level mechanism and a measure on the way back up. If you cannot draw both, you have a slogan, not a design.

hinge.q: 'Productive failure contradicts Kirschner, Sweller & Clark.' Which is the best assessment?
options: Mostly false: PF includes explicit consolidation and targets learners with prior knowledge, so it keeps the core mechanism and disagrees on sequencing
True for mathematics, false for science, because inquiry is the method of science and procedures are the substance of mathematics at school level
False; they agree entirely, because both accept that explicit instruction is needed and differ only in how they describe it
True; you must pick a side, because one camp says struggle before instruction helps novices and the other says it harms them, and both cannot be right
diagnoses: Correct. Kirschner, Sweller & Clark attack minimal guidance; PF is generate-then-instruct with scripted consolidation, beneficial for conceptual understanding and transfer and not for procedures.
Domain reading. The boundary is goal type and prior knowledge, not the subject.
False harmony. They genuinely differ on how much struggle before instruction helps, and on where the prior-knowledge threshold sits.
Winner-take-all reading. The debate resolves by conditions (goal, prior knowledge, consolidation), not by a winner.

hinge.q: Which is the correct chain from institution to mind for the policy 'all teachers use hinge questions'?
options: Students see that teachers care about their understanding, so motivation rises, and motivated students learn more from any lesson they are given
The institution mandates it, teachers comply, and students learn more because every class now checks understanding every lesson, closing the policy-practice gap
TLCs build the habit; the hinge makes each student's thinking visible; the teacher's next move adapts; instruction matches each student's current schema
Hinge questions test students, and testing improves memory, because every retrieval strengthens the trace that was just retrieved, in every classroom
diagnoses: Affective-only reading. Relationship matters, but it is not the mechanism by which a hinge question improves learning.
Mandate theory. Mandates produce surface compliance and lethal mutations; habit change needs the TLC structure.
Correct. Each link names the band and mechanism: adult learning, elicitation, contingent teaching, and the prior-knowledge and working-memory constraints in minds.
Retrieval-only reading. True as far as it goes, but it misses the main mechanism, which is the adaptive decision the evidence enables.

hinge.q: Your brief says: 'Small classes improve learning.' What is the correct tag, and why?
options: [E], because it is obvious: fewer students means more attention for each, and no study is needed to establish what every teacher knows
[V], because class size is a values choice: a school that wants every child known chooses small classes whatever the test scores say
[H], because nobody has studied it properly: the trials are old, from one state, and say nothing about a new school with its own teachers and families
[E] with a caveat: the effects are real (strongest in early grades) but modest and expensive relative to alternatives, and they shrink at scale
diagnoses: Obviousness as evidence. The tag is right only by luck; the reasoning would let any intuition pass as evidence.
Over-tagging V to avoid scrutiny. There is strong evidence about class size; a value may also be involved, but it does not replace the evidence.
Ignorance of the literature. Class size is among the most studied questions in education.
Correct. Tennessee STAR supports a real effect; California shows dilution at scale; the strategic question is cost per unit of learning. If parents value being known, that part is a separate [V].

hinge.q: At a community design session, families propose replacing systematic phonics in K-2 with a 'balanced literacy' approach they saw at a neighboring school. Under your standardization-vs-codesign rule, you:
options: Adopt it, because community ownership is essential to survival and a school that overrides families on early reading will lose the coalition it depends on by the end of Year 2
Recognize a proposal to change a mechanism the compact fixes by evidence, then surface the need behind it and meet it in the open layer: read-alouds, rich texts, library
End community codesign, because families should not shape the school's teaching and this proposal shows exactly where open input leads a school
Run a PDSA cycle comparing phonics with balanced literacy in two classes, because a local test with practical measures settles it for this community
diagnoses: Voice-validates-mechanism. Early reading mechanics are one of the most settled areas in the curriculum; adopting this would harm children.
Correct. The compact says which layer is open. The need behind the proposal is real and answerable without abandoning the mechanism.
Throwing out the signal. Codesign is how you learn needs and build the coalition that sustains the school; the fix is governance of layers, not abolition.
Misuse of PDSA. Improvement cycles implement settled science locally; they are not for re-testing it on children who cannot be rolled back.

hinge.q: Your brief says: 'Every core course ends each term in an authentic product for a real audience, which will deepen learning.' What is the best tag?
options: [H], because it rests on a strong but observational, selection-confounded pattern, and needs testing in your core courses with practical measures
Delete it, because there is no evidence at all: no study has measured learning from authentic products, so the claim cannot stand in a brief
[E], because Mehta & Fine showed it: across thirty schools, depth appeared wherever students made real products for real audiences
[V], because authenticity is a preference: a school may choose real audiences for its own reasons, but that choice is not an empirical claim at all
diagnoses: Correct. It is a well-grounded hypothesis. Register it with a first test and a switch signal, such as mastery checks on the disciplinary content inside the product.
Overcorrection. The periphery pattern, apprenticeship research and motivation research make it a reasonable bet; weak evidence is not no evidence.
